Geography: teach from the board

Select a lesson. These are the same explanations available through Read teaching script on every lesson screen. Read or adapt them while teaching. Use Print selected lesson for a paper teaching script.

The 40-minute route contains a geographical question, vocabulary, full subject explanations, worked examples, explained cases, brief spoken checks and a recap. Students can follow the entire lesson without copying notes. Print a matching worksheet only if you want written consolidation.

Timings are planning estimates. Classroom teaching duration has not been measured; the guide contains substantive explanations rather than instructions to prolong a short activity.

Landscape detectives

7A · Week 2 · sections 1.1

40-minute planning estimate: introduction 3, goal 2, vocabulary 3, explanation 17, worked examples 7, case explanation 4, spoken checks 3, recap 1. Divide each block between topics in combined lessons. Adjust to the class; elapsed classroom teaching time has not been measured.

0–3 min · Introduce the geographical question

Why a bridge is more than a building

On screen: Which question asks about location?

Picture a river between homes and a school. The water, valley and banks are physical features. The bridge and school are human features.

3–5 min · What this lesson explains

Classify a feature and explain an interaction

On screen: Follow the map, diagram and explanation. / No copying is needed. The printed sheet is optional. / What is here? Where is it? / Physical: river, hill, soil. / Rain can affect a road.

This lesson explains how to describe physical and human features and explain their links. The worked example shows the method, and the scheduled case shows how it applies to a different situation. Read the three geographical ideas aloud, then connect each one to a feature in the visual. Students can follow the demonstration without producing a written answer.

5–8 min · Make the words clear

Words we will use

On screen: Physical geography: Natural features and processes / Human geography: People, places and activities / Interaction: How people and nature affect each other

Physical geography means natural features and processes. Soil and plants in a school garden.

Human geography means people, places and activities. People build and use the path.

Interaction means how people and nature affect each other. A pupil waters the plants.

8–25 min · Teach the Geography

Geography asks about places

On screen: What is here? Where is it? / Why is it here? How does it affect people?

Geography helps us understand places and the connections between them. Start with our classroom. The building has a location, people use it, and its surroundings influence how we reach it. Now move out to the school, the town and the world. These are different scales of study. A question about one street needs local detail; a question about countries needs a wider view. Geography joins information about nature and people rather than treating a place as a list of names.

Brief check: Which question asks about location?
Listen for: “Where is it?” asks about location.

Physical and human features

On screen: Physical: river, hill, soil. / Human: road, bridge, building.

Physical geography studies natural features and processes. Human geography studies people and their activities. Point to the river and describe its water and banks. Then point to the bridge and describe what people built. A feature can involve both. A farm uses soil, plants and rainfall, but people choose crops and manage the land. Do not tell pupils that every feature must fit only one box. The categories help us explain a place; they do not remove the connections between its parts.

Brief check: Why can a farm involve both categories?
Listen for: Natural soil and rainfall support human farming activities.

People and nature affect each other

On screen: Rain can affect a road. / A road can affect rainwater flow.

An interaction is a connection in which things affect each other. Heavy rain can make a road difficult to use. Building a road can also change the ground: a paved surface may allow less water into soil, so more water may move over the surface. Trace each direction with an arrow. The first starts with a natural process and ends with a human activity. The second starts with construction and ends with water movement. We need evidence to find the size of an effect in a real place.

Brief check: Can the connection work in both directions?
Listen for: Yes. Nature affects people, and people change their environment.

Explain a connection

On screen: Name the feature and the change. / Use “because” or “so”.

Compare two sentences. “River, bridge, school” lists three features. “The bridge crosses the river, so pupils can reach the school from the other bank” explains a connection. Point to each feature while saying its part of the sentence. The word so joins an action to an effect. Because introduces a reason. A useful geographical explanation tells us how the connection works. “The bridge is good” gives a judgement without explaining it. Ask the class which words show what the bridge actually does.

Brief check: What is missing from a list of features?
Listen for: The action or process connecting them.

Why a bridge is more than a building

On screen: Picture a river between homes and a school. / The bridge is human-made, but its effects involve the river, plants and people.

Picture a river between homes and a school. The water, valley and banks are physical features. The bridge and school are human features. A bridge connects the two banks, allowing people to cross without entering the water. Its construction may also remove vegetation or alter the banks. Geography follows both connections: what people gain from the crossing and what changes in the environment.

The bridge is human-made, but its effects involve the river, plants and people. A useful explanation joins them: building a crossing can shorten a journey because people no longer need to travel to a distant bridge. The actual time saved would need a route measurement.

A reservoir contains water, but a dam built by people changes its storage. Name the natural feature, the human action and the effect; do not force every example into one box.

Vegetation is natural material; planting and shelter are human action and purpose.

The bridge is human-made, but its effects involve the river, plants and people. A useful explanation joins them: building a crossing can shorten a journey because people no longer need to travel to a distant bridge. The actual time saved would need a route measurement.

Response A: People change vegetation to reduce wind exposure.

Vegetation is natural material; planting and shelter are human action and purpose.

A useful explanation joins them: building a crossing can shorten a journey because people no longer need to travel to a distant bridge. The actual time saved would need a route measurement.

5–8 min · Make the words clear

Words we will use

On screen: Physical geography: Natural features and processes / Human geography: People, places and activities / Interaction: How people and nature affect each other

Physical geography means natural features and processes. Soil and plants in a school garden.

Human geography means people, places and activities. People build and use the path.

Interaction means how people and nature affect each other. A pupil waters the plants.

Words we will use

On screen: Atlas: A collection of maps / Compass: A tool that shows direction / Scale: The link between map and real distance

Atlas means a collection of maps. An atlas index helps locate Brazil.

Compass means a tool that shows direction. A compass helps find north.

Scale means the link between map and real distance. At 1 cm = 10 m, 3 cm represents 30 m.

Compare two sentences. “River, bridge, school” lists three features. “The bridge crosses the river, so pupils can reach the school from the other bank” explains a connection. Listen for: The action or process connecting them.

Why a bridge is more than a building

On screen: Picture a river between homes and a school. / The bridge is human-made, but its effects involve the river, plants and people.

Picture a river between homes and a school. The water, valley and banks are physical features. The bridge and school are human features. A bridge connects the two banks, allowing people to cross without entering the water. Its construction may also remove vegetation or alter the banks. Geography follows both connections: what people gain from the crossing and what changes in the environment.

The bridge is human-made, but its effects involve the river, plants and people. A useful explanation joins them: building a crossing can shorten a journey because people no longer need to travel to a distant bridge. The actual time saved would need a route measurement.

Match a tool to a question

On screen: Location: map or atlas. / Direction: north arrow or compass.

Begin with the question before choosing a tool. An atlas contains maps and an index that helps us find places. A compass helps identify direction. A ruler measures a line, but does not tell us which country we are looking at. Show how the same place can be investigated in several ways. To locate it, use a map; to describe its appearance, use a photograph; to estimate a mapped distance, use a ruler and the map scale. No single tool answers every geographical question.

Brief check: Can a ruler tell us which way is north?
Listen for: No. A ruler measures length; direction needs another reference.

Read a map carefully

On screen: Find the title, key and north arrow. / Check the scale before measuring.

A map is a selective drawing of a place. Its title tells us the area or topic. The key explains symbols and colours. The north arrow gives direction, and the scale connects the drawing to real distances. Demonstrate this order before identifying individual features. A blue line might represent a river, but we should confirm it using the key. A large symbol may be easy to see without showing the feature’s exact size. Reading the supporting information prevents us from guessing from appearance alone.

Brief check: Why should we read the key?
Listen for: It tells us what this map’s symbols mean.

Measure and convert

On screen: Start at the ruler’s zero mark. / Map length × scale = ground distance.

Place the zero mark at the start of the line, not the edge of the ruler. State the map measurement in centimetres. If the scale says one centimetre represents forty metres, each centimetre is one equal forty-metre section. A three-centimetre path represents three times forty, or one hundred and twenty metres. The units change because we move from the drawing to the ground. Adding three and forty would mix different quantities. Show the three equal sections before writing the multiplication.

Brief check: Why do we multiply rather than add?
Listen for: Each map centimetre represents another equal section of ground distance.

Record a result others can check

On screen: Name the feature, result and unit. / Say which tool or source you used.

“It is four” is not a complete geographical record. We do not know what was measured or what four means. “Path B measures four centimetres on this map” identifies the object, number and unit. Add the scale when calculating the ground distance. A photograph also needs a place and date if it is used to show change. Clear records let another person check the method instead of trusting an unexplained answer. Model a weak record and improve it aloud, keeping the original visible for comparison.

Brief check: What information is missing from “It is four”?
Listen for: The feature, unit and method are missing.

A photograph cannot measure everything

On screen: Imagine a survey team with a photograph, compass, atlas and ruler. / In our invented map, one centimetre represents 50 metres.

Imagine a survey team with a photograph, compass, atlas and ruler. The photograph shows a path curving past a tree. It records visible appearance, but without a known scale it cannot establish the path’s real length. A compass supplies direction. An atlas helps locate places. A ruler measures a line on a map; the scale converts that measurement into ground distance. Different tools answer different questions.

In our invented map, one centimetre represents 50 metres. A six-centimetre path represents 6 × 50 = 300 metres. Start the ruler at zero, trace the whole route and state both the unit and the scale. Measuring six centimetres is only the first step.

Change the example · 1.2

5–8 min · Make the words clear

Words we will use

On screen: Atlas: A collection of maps / Compass: A tool that shows direction / Scale: The link between map and real distance

Atlas means a collection of maps. An atlas index helps locate Brazil.

Compass means a tool that shows direction. A compass helps find north.

Scale means the link between map and real distance. At 1 cm = 10 m, 3 cm represents 30 m.

8–25 min · Teach the Geography

Match a tool to a question

On screen: Location: map or atlas. / Direction: north arrow or compass.

Begin with the question before choosing a tool. An atlas contains maps and an index that helps us find places. A compass helps identify direction. A ruler measures a line, but does not tell us which country we are looking at. Show how the same place can be investigated in several ways. To locate it, use a map; to describe its appearance, use a photograph; to estimate a mapped distance, use a ruler and the map scale. No single tool answers every geographical question.

Brief check: Can a ruler tell us which way is north?
Listen for: No. A ruler measures length; direction needs another reference.

Read a map carefully

On screen: Find the title, key and north arrow. / Check the scale before measuring.

A map is a selective drawing of a place. Its title tells us the area or topic. The key explains symbols and colours. The north arrow gives direction, and the scale connects the drawing to real distances. Demonstrate this order before identifying individual features. A blue line might represent a river, but we should confirm it using the key. A large symbol may be easy to see without showing the feature’s exact size. Reading the supporting information prevents us from guessing from appearance alone.

Brief check: Why should we read the key?
Listen for: It tells us what this map’s symbols mean.

Measure and convert

On screen: Start at the ruler’s zero mark. / Map length × scale = ground distance.

Place the zero mark at the start of the line, not the edge of the ruler. State the map measurement in centimetres. If the scale says one centimetre represents forty metres, each centimetre is one equal forty-metre section. A three-centimetre path represents three times forty, or one hundred and twenty metres. The units change because we move from the drawing to the ground. Adding three and forty would mix different quantities. Show the three equal sections before writing the multiplication.

Brief check: Why do we multiply rather than add?
Listen for: Each map centimetre represents another equal section of ground distance.

Record a result others can check

On screen: Name the feature, result and unit. / Say which tool or source you used.

“It is four” is not a complete geographical record. We do not know what was measured or what four means. “Path B measures four centimetres on this map” identifies the object, number and unit. Add the scale when calculating the ground distance. A photograph also needs a place and date if it is used to show change. Clear records let another person check the method instead of trusting an unexplained answer. Model a weak record and improve it aloud, keeping the original visible for comparison.

Brief check: What information is missing from “It is four”?
Listen for: The feature, unit and method are missing.

Two queues: a clue rather than a verdict

On screen: Does a long queue prove a shop is popular?

5–8 min · Make the words clear

Words we will use

On screen: Observation: Something you see or measure / Evidence: Information supporting an answer / Enquiry: A question investigated with evidence

Observation means something you see or measure. Eight pupils wait at Door A.

Evidence means information supporting an answer. A timed count supports a queue comparison.

Enquiry means a question investigated with evidence. Do the queues differ at the same time each day?

8–25 min · Teach the Geography

Observation and inference

On screen: Observation: what we can see or measure. / Inference: a possible explanation.

An observation comes from a source or measurement. If a photograph shows a queue, we can describe the people visible. Saying that everyone likes the shop is an inference: it suggests a reason that the photograph does not establish. Other reasons are possible, such as slow service or a special event. Use a familiar classroom example before returning to the geographical image. Keep observations and proposed explanations in different columns. This allows pupils to offer ideas while still understanding which claims have actually been checked.

Brief check: Does a long queue prove a shop is popular?
Listen for: No. Popularity is one possible explanation; other reasons could produce a queue.

Make a question measurable

On screen: Choose one place or feature. / Decide what you will count or measure.

“Is our school good?” is too broad for a simple geographical enquiry. “How many people use each gate in five minutes?” tells us what to observe, where and for how long. Explain how a count differs from an opinion. We can count people crossing a line, but happiness requires a different kind of evidence. A good question helps us choose an appropriate method. Before starting, agree exactly what counts as an entry so two observers would make comparable records.

Brief check: Which is easier to investigate: “good school” or “people using each gate”?
Listen for: The gate question gives a clear, countable outcome.

Make comparisons fair

On screen: Use the same counting time. / Use the same rule at each place.

Suppose we count one gate for five minutes and another for ten. The second may have a larger count because we watched longer, not because it is busier. Hold the counting time constant. We also need the same rule for entering and leaving, and comparable observation times. A bag on the boundary between two survey areas should be counted according to one agreed rule. Fairness here means controlling the method so the difference we report is meaningful. It is not about making all results equal.

Brief check: Why could different counting times mislead us?
Listen for: The longer observation has more opportunity to record people.

Repeat before making a broad claim

On screen: A count describes one time. / Repeated counts can reveal variation.

One count is a snapshot. A gate that is busy on Monday may be quieter on Tuesday. Show two days with different results and calculate the combined counts. Discuss why weather, events or lesson times might affect movement, without claiming we know the cause. Repeating a measurement makes us less dependent on one unusual moment. Even repeated counts at two gates do not automatically describe every entrance or every season. A conclusion should name the places and times studied and explain what remains unknown.

Brief check: Does one busy morning prove a gate is always busiest?
Listen for: No. We need comparable repeated observations.

Two queues: a clue rather than a verdict

On screen: At the same moment, eight pupils wait at Door A and two wait at Door B. / A fair investigation repeats counts at both doors over equal time periods, using the same rule for who counts as waiting.

At the same moment, eight pupils wait at Door A and two wait at Door B. We can observe a difference of six pupils. We cannot yet conclude that Door A is badly designed: a lesson may have just ended nearby, one doorway may be closed, or the queues may change a minute later. An observation states what was counted. An inference offers an explanation for it.

A fair investigation repeats counts at both doors over equal time periods, using the same rule for who counts as waiting. Compare similar days and record unusual events. A repeated pattern strengthens a description; explaining its cause still requires evidence about what differs between the doorways.

5–8 min · Make the words clear

Words we will use

On screen: Physical geography: Natural features and processes / Human geography: People, places and activities / Interaction: How people and nature affect each other

Physical geography means natural features and processes. Soil and plants in a school garden.

Human geography means people, places and activities. People build and use the path.

Interaction means how people and nature affect each other. A pupil waters the plants.

Words we will use

On screen: Atlas: A collection of maps / Compass: A tool that shows direction / Scale: The link between map and real distance

Atlas means a collection of maps. An atlas index helps locate Brazil.

Compass means a tool that shows direction. A compass helps find north.

Scale means the link between map and real distance. At 1 cm = 10 m, 3 cm represents 30 m.

Words we will use

On screen: Observation: Something you see or measure / Evidence: Information supporting an answer / Enquiry: A question investigated with evidence

Observation means something you see or measure. Eight pupils wait at Door A.

Evidence means information supporting an answer. A timed count supports a queue comparison.

Enquiry means a question investigated with evidence. Do the queues differ at the same time each day?

8–25 min · Reconnect and explain

Geography asks about places

On screen: What is here? Where is it? / Why is it here? How does it affect people?

Geography helps us understand places and the connections between them. Start with our classroom. The building has a location, people use it, and its surroundings influence how we reach it. Now move out to the school, the town and the world. These are different scales of study. A question about one street needs local detail; a question about countries needs a wider view. Geography joins information about nature and people rather than treating a place as a list of names.

Brief check: Which question asks about location?
Listen for: “Where is it?” asks about location.

People and nature affect each other

On screen: Rain can affect a road. / A road can affect rainwater flow.

An interaction is a connection in which things affect each other. Heavy rain can make a road difficult to use. Building a road can also change the ground: a paved surface may allow less water into soil, so more water may move over the surface. Trace each direction with an arrow. The first starts with a natural process and ends with a human activity. The second starts with construction and ends with water movement. We need evidence to find the size of an effect in a real place.

Brief check: Can the connection work in both directions?
Listen for: Yes. Nature affects people, and people change their environment.

Explain a connection

On screen: Name the feature and the change. / Use “because” or “so”.

Compare two sentences. “River, bridge, school” lists three features. “The bridge crosses the river, so pupils can reach the school from the other bank” explains a connection. Point to each feature while saying its part of the sentence. The word so joins an action to an effect. Because introduces a reason. A useful geographical explanation tells us how the connection works. “The bridge is good” gives a judgement without explaining it. Ask the class which words show what the bridge actually does.

Brief check: What is missing from a list of features?
Listen for: The action or process connecting them.

Why a bridge is more than a building

On screen: Picture a river between homes and a school. / The bridge is human-made, but its effects involve the river, plants and people.

Picture a river between homes and a school. The water, valley and banks are physical features. The bridge and school are human features. A bridge connects the two banks, allowing people to cross without entering the water. Its construction may also remove vegetation or alter the banks. Geography follows both connections: what people gain from the crossing and what changes in the environment.

The bridge is human-made, but its effects involve the river, plants and people. A useful explanation joins them: building a crossing can shorten a journey because people no longer need to travel to a distant bridge. The actual time saved would need a route measurement.

Match a tool to a question

On screen: Location: map or atlas. / Direction: north arrow or compass.

Begin with the question before choosing a tool. An atlas contains maps and an index that helps us find places. A compass helps identify direction. A ruler measures a line, but does not tell us which country we are looking at. Show how the same place can be investigated in several ways. To locate it, use a map; to describe its appearance, use a photograph; to estimate a mapped distance, use a ruler and the map scale. No single tool answers every geographical question.

Brief check: Can a ruler tell us which way is north?
Listen for: No. A ruler measures length; direction needs another reference.

Measure and convert

On screen: Start at the ruler’s zero mark. / Map length × scale = ground distance.

Place the zero mark at the start of the line, not the edge of the ruler. State the map measurement in centimetres. If the scale says one centimetre represents forty metres, each centimetre is one equal forty-metre section. A three-centimetre path represents three times forty, or one hundred and twenty metres. The units change because we move from the drawing to the ground. Adding three and forty would mix different quantities. Show the three equal sections before writing the multiplication.

Brief check: Why do we multiply rather than add?
Listen for: Each map centimetre represents another equal section of ground distance.

Record a result others can check

On screen: Name the feature, result and unit. / Say which tool or source you used.

“It is four” is not a complete geographical record. We do not know what was measured or what four means. “Path B measures four centimetres on this map” identifies the object, number and unit. Add the scale when calculating the ground distance. A photograph also needs a place and date if it is used to show change. Clear records let another person check the method instead of trusting an unexplained answer. Model a weak record and improve it aloud, keeping the original visible for comparison.

Brief check: What information is missing from “It is four”?
Listen for: The feature, unit and method are missing.

A photograph cannot measure everything

On screen: Imagine a survey team with a photograph, compass, atlas and ruler. / In our invented map, one centimetre represents 50 metres.

Imagine a survey team with a photograph, compass, atlas and ruler. The photograph shows a path curving past a tree. It records visible appearance, but without a known scale it cannot establish the path’s real length. A compass supplies direction. An atlas helps locate places. A ruler measures a line on a map; the scale converts that measurement into ground distance. Different tools answer different questions.

In our invented map, one centimetre represents 50 metres. A six-centimetre path represents 6 × 50 = 300 metres. Start the ruler at zero, trace the whole route and state both the unit and the scale. Measuring six centimetres is only the first step.

Observation and inference

On screen: Observation: what we can see or measure. / Inference: a possible explanation.

An observation comes from a source or measurement. If a photograph shows a queue, we can describe the people visible. Saying that everyone likes the shop is an inference: it suggests a reason that the photograph does not establish. Other reasons are possible, such as slow service or a special event. Use a familiar classroom example before returning to the geographical image. Keep observations and proposed explanations in different columns. This allows pupils to offer ideas while still understanding which claims have actually been checked.

Brief check: Does a long queue prove a shop is popular?
Listen for: No. Popularity is one possible explanation; other reasons could produce a queue.

Make comparisons fair

On screen: Use the same counting time. / Use the same rule at each place.

Suppose we count one gate for five minutes and another for ten. The second may have a larger count because we watched longer, not because it is busier. Hold the counting time constant. We also need the same rule for entering and leaving, and comparable observation times. A bag on the boundary between two survey areas should be counted according to one agreed rule. Fairness here means controlling the method so the difference we report is meaningful. It is not about making all results equal.

Brief check: Why could different counting times mislead us?
Listen for: The longer observation has more opportunity to record people.

Repeat before making a broad claim

On screen: A count describes one time. / Repeated counts can reveal variation.

One count is a snapshot. A gate that is busy on Monday may be quieter on Tuesday. Show two days with different results and calculate the combined counts. Discuss why weather, events or lesson times might affect movement, without claiming we know the cause. Repeating a measurement makes us less dependent on one unusual moment. Even repeated counts at two gates do not automatically describe every entrance or every season. A conclusion should name the places and times studied and explain what remains unknown.

Brief check: Does one busy morning prove a gate is always busiest?
Listen for: No. We need comparable repeated observations.

Two queues: a clue rather than a verdict

On screen: At the same moment, eight pupils wait at Door A and two wait at Door B. / A fair investigation repeats counts at both doors over equal time periods, using the same rule for who counts as waiting.

At the same moment, eight pupils wait at Door A and two wait at Door B. We can observe a difference of six pupils. We cannot yet conclude that Door A is badly designed: a lesson may have just ended nearby, one doorway may be closed, or the queues may change a minute later. An observation states what was counted. An inference offers an explanation for it.

A fair investigation repeats counts at both doors over equal time periods, using the same rule for who counts as waiting. Compare similar days and record unusual events. A repeated pattern strengthens a description; explaining its cause still requires evidence about what differs between the doorways.

5–8 min · Make the words clear

Words we will use

On screen: Observation: Something you see or measure / Evidence: Information supporting an answer / Enquiry: A question investigated with evidence

Observation means something you see or measure. Eight pupils wait at Door A.

Evidence means information supporting an answer. A timed count supports a queue comparison.

Enquiry means a question investigated with evidence. Do the queues differ at the same time each day?

Words we will use

On screen: Land use: How people use an area / Industry: Making goods and providing services / Change: A difference between two times

Land use means how people use an area. Fields can become housing.

Industry means making goods and providing services. Workshops make or repair goods.

Change means a difference between two times. A ferry crossing is replaced by a bridge.

8–25 min · Teach the Geography

Observation and inference

On screen: Observation: what we can see or measure. / Inference: a possible explanation.

An observation comes from a source or measurement. If a photograph shows a queue, we can describe the people visible. Saying that everyone likes the shop is an inference: it suggests a reason that the photograph does not establish. Other reasons are possible, such as slow service or a special event. Use a familiar classroom example before returning to the geographical image. Keep observations and proposed explanations in different columns. This allows pupils to offer ideas while still understanding which claims have actually been checked.

Brief check: Does a long queue prove a shop is popular?
Listen for: No. Popularity is one possible explanation; other reasons could produce a queue.

Make a question measurable

On screen: Choose one place or feature. / Decide what you will count or measure.

“Is our school good?” is too broad for a simple geographical enquiry. “How many people use each gate in five minutes?” tells us what to observe, where and for how long. Explain how a count differs from an opinion. We can count people crossing a line, but happiness requires a different kind of evidence. A good question helps us choose an appropriate method. Before starting, agree exactly what counts as an entry so two observers would make comparable records.

Brief check: Which is easier to investigate: “good school” or “people using each gate”?
Listen for: The gate question gives a clear, countable outcome.

Make comparisons fair

On screen: Use the same counting time. / Use the same rule at each place.

Suppose we count one gate for five minutes and another for ten. The second may have a larger count because we watched longer, not because it is busier. Hold the counting time constant. We also need the same rule for entering and leaving, and comparable observation times. A bag on the boundary between two survey areas should be counted according to one agreed rule. Fairness here means controlling the method so the difference we report is meaningful. It is not about making all results equal.

Brief check: Why could different counting times mislead us?
Listen for: The longer observation has more opportunity to record people.

Repeat before making a broad claim

On screen: A count describes one time. / Repeated counts can reveal variation.

One count is a snapshot. A gate that is busy on Monday may be quieter on Tuesday. Show two days with different results and calculate the combined counts. Discuss why weather, events or lesson times might affect movement, without claiming we know the cause. Repeating a measurement makes us less dependent on one unusual moment. Even repeated counts at two gates do not automatically describe every entrance or every season. A conclusion should name the places and times studied and explain what remains unknown.

Brief check: Does one busy morning prove a gate is always busiest?
Listen for: No. We need comparable repeated observations.

Two queues: a clue rather than a verdict

On screen: At the same moment, eight pupils wait at Door A and two wait at Door B. / A fair investigation repeats counts at both doors over equal time periods, using the same rule for who counts as waiting.

At the same moment, eight pupils wait at Door A and two wait at Door B. We can observe a difference of six pupils. We cannot yet conclude that Door A is badly designed: a lesson may have just ended nearby, one doorway may be closed, or the queues may change a minute later. An observation states what was counted. An inference offers an explanation for it.

A fair investigation repeats counts at both doors over equal time periods, using the same rule for who counts as waiting. Compare similar days and record unusual events. A repeated pattern strengthens a description; explaining its cause still requires evidence about what differs between the doorways.

Ironbridge Gorge: a changing industrial landscape

On screen: Ironbridge Gorge is in Shropshire, beside the River Severn. / Industry, transport and settlement changed the landscape.

Ironbridge Gorge is a real place in Shropshire associated with the Industrial Revolution. The River Severn runs through the gorge. Its historic industrial landscape includes evidence of manufacturing, transport and homes, while the iron bridge is an important example of early large-scale structural use of cast iron. Explain why this is more than a story about one bridge: industry changes land use, creates connections between workplaces and housing, and leaves material traces. Today, historical remains can also serve heritage and visitor purposes. Use this factual background to introduce change, while keeping our imagined before-and-after drawings separate from verified historical records. We can practise comparison with a schematic, but cannot use invented building counts to describe the actual gorge’s history.

Brief check: Why should the fictional drawing’s counts not become historical Ironbridge facts?
Listen for: They are classroom data rather than historical records.

Places change over time

On screen: Look at the same place on two dates. / Separate what stayed from what changed.

A place can change in its buildings, transport, land use and environment. Put two views of the same place side by side. Start with a feature that appears in both so pupils know they are comparing the same area. Then identify a feature added, removed or altered. A stayed-and-changed table prevents us from treating the whole place as new. Dates matter: an undated photograph can show appearance, but cannot reliably establish which view came first. Keep imagined classroom scenes separate from verified historical photographs.

Brief check: Why do the dates matter?
Listen for: They establish the order of the changes.

A crossing changes access

On screen: A ferry crosses water in separate trips. / A bridge provides a fixed crossing when open.

A river can connect places by water while also making travel between its banks difficult. A ferry carries people or goods in trips. A bridge creates a fixed crossing, but it still needs suitable access and can close. Trace a journey before and after a crossing is added. Explain the mechanism: a shorter or more reliable route may make a destination easier to reach. We should not leap from a bridge symbol to a precise claim about jobs or income; those require separate records.

Brief check: What can a new crossing change directly?
Listen for: The routes people can use to move between the banks.

Describe first, explain second

On screen: “A workshop appeared” describes change. / “Access may have helped” suggests a cause.

Descriptions tell us what differs between the sources. Explanations suggest why that difference occurred. A new workshop beside a bridge may lead us to ask whether improved access helped the business. Its location alone does not prove that cause. The workshop might have opened for another reason or before the bridge. Demonstrate both sentence types using the same image. Accurate description is the starting point; a causal explanation needs evidence linking the change in transport to the change in activity.

Brief check: Does being close to a bridge prove a business opened because of it?
Listen for: No. Location alone does not establish cause.

Test the proposed cause

On screen: A cause must come before its effect. / Use dates, records and comparisons.

If a shop opened in 2015 and the bridge opened in 2020, the bridge cannot explain the shop’s original opening. It could still affect later customer numbers. Split those two claims rather than accepting or rejecting everything at once. To investigate later effects, compare suitable records before and after the crossing, and consider other changes. This is how historical geography joins the story of a place to evidence. A convincing explanation identifies a possible mechanism and checks whether the timing and records support it.

Brief check: What does an earlier shop opening rule out?
Listen for: The later bridge cannot have caused that original opening.

What changes when a crossing opens?

On screen: Imagine two drawings of the same riverbank, five years apart. / The drawings alone do not prove that the bridge caused every new building.

Imagine two drawings of the same riverbank, five years apart. The earlier drawing shows a ferry landing and fields. The later one shows a bridge, a road and new shops. First describe the visible changes: transport infrastructure and land use have changed. Then suggest a connection: a permanent road crossing may make this bank easier to reach and attract customers.

The drawings alone do not prove that the bridge caused every new building. Planning decisions, population growth or another new road could also matter. Compare the dates of the changes and seek evidence about journeys and businesses. Keep this invented example separate from the real industrial history of Ironbridge Gorge.

We cannot yet conclude that Door A is badly designed: a lesson may have just ended nearby, one doorway may be closed, or the queues may change a minute later. An observation states what was counted. An inference offers an explanation for it.

A fair investigation repeats counts at both doors over equal time periods, using the same rule for who counts as waiting. Compare similar days and record unusual events. A repeated pattern strengthens a description; explaining its cause still requires evidence about what differs between the doorways.

Does one busy morning prove a gate is always busiest?

On screen: Think about the explanation. Answer aloud when invited.

5–8 min · Make the words clear

Words we will use

On screen: Land use: How people use an area / Industry: Making goods and providing services / Change: A difference between two times

Land use means how people use an area. Fields can become housing.

Industry means making goods and providing services. Workshops make or repair goods.

Change means a difference between two times. A ferry crossing is replaced by a bridge.

8–25 min · Teach the Geography

Ironbridge Gorge: a changing industrial landscape

On screen: Ironbridge Gorge is in Shropshire, beside the River Severn. / Industry, transport and settlement changed the landscape.

Ironbridge Gorge is a real place in Shropshire associated with the Industrial Revolution. The River Severn runs through the gorge. Its historic industrial landscape includes evidence of manufacturing, transport and homes, while the iron bridge is an important example of early large-scale structural use of cast iron. Explain why this is more than a story about one bridge: industry changes land use, creates connections between workplaces and housing, and leaves material traces. Today, historical remains can also serve heritage and visitor purposes. Use this factual background to introduce change, while keeping our imagined before-and-after drawings separate from verified historical records. We can practise comparison with a schematic, but cannot use invented building counts to describe the actual gorge’s history.

Brief check: Why should the fictional drawing’s counts not become historical Ironbridge facts?
Listen for: They are classroom data rather than historical records.

Places change over time

On screen: Look at the same place on two dates. / Separate what stayed from what changed.

A place can change in its buildings, transport, land use and environment. Put two views of the same place side by side. Start with a feature that appears in both so pupils know they are comparing the same area. Then identify a feature added, removed or altered. A stayed-and-changed table prevents us from treating the whole place as new. Dates matter: an undated photograph can show appearance, but cannot reliably establish which view came first. Keep imagined classroom scenes separate from verified historical photographs.

Brief check: Why do the dates matter?
Listen for: They establish the order of the changes.

A crossing changes access

On screen: A ferry crosses water in separate trips. / A bridge provides a fixed crossing when open.

A river can connect places by water while also making travel between its banks difficult. A ferry carries people or goods in trips. A bridge creates a fixed crossing, but it still needs suitable access and can close. Trace a journey before and after a crossing is added. Explain the mechanism: a shorter or more reliable route may make a destination easier to reach. We should not leap from a bridge symbol to a precise claim about jobs or income; those require separate records.

Brief check: What can a new crossing change directly?
Listen for: The routes people can use to move between the banks.

Describe first, explain second

On screen: “A workshop appeared” describes change. / “Access may have helped” suggests a cause.

Descriptions tell us what differs between the sources. Explanations suggest why that difference occurred. A new workshop beside a bridge may lead us to ask whether improved access helped the business. Its location alone does not prove that cause. The workshop might have opened for another reason or before the bridge. Demonstrate both sentence types using the same image. Accurate description is the starting point; a causal explanation needs evidence linking the change in transport to the change in activity.

Brief check: Does being close to a bridge prove a business opened because of it?
Listen for: No. Location alone does not establish cause.

Test the proposed cause

On screen: A cause must come before its effect. / Use dates, records and comparisons.

If a shop opened in 2015 and the bridge opened in 2020, the bridge cannot explain the shop’s original opening. It could still affect later customer numbers. Split those two claims rather than accepting or rejecting everything at once. To investigate later effects, compare suitable records before and after the crossing, and consider other changes. This is how historical geography joins the story of a place to evidence. A convincing explanation identifies a possible mechanism and checks whether the timing and records support it.

Brief check: What does an earlier shop opening rule out?
Listen for: The later bridge cannot have caused that original opening.

What changes when a crossing opens?

On screen: Imagine two drawings of the same riverbank, five years apart. / The drawings alone do not prove that the bridge caused every new building.

Imagine two drawings of the same riverbank, five years apart. The earlier drawing shows a ferry landing and fields. The later one shows a bridge, a road and new shops. First describe the visible changes: transport infrastructure and land use have changed. Then suggest a connection: a permanent road crossing may make this bank easier to reach and attract customers.

The drawings alone do not prove that the bridge caused every new building. Planning decisions, population growth or another new road could also matter. Compare the dates of the changes and seek evidence about journeys and businesses. Keep this invented example separate from the real industrial history of Ironbridge Gorge.

On screen: Follow the map, diagram and explanation. / No copying is needed. The printed sheet is optional. / Give the requested feature. / Use position, shape and number. / Give a reason or process.

This lesson explains how to answer the command word in a geography question. The worked example shows the method, and the scheduled case shows how it applies to a different situation. 5–8 min · Make the words clear

Words we will use

On screen: Identify: Name the feature / Describe: Say what it is like / Explain: Give a reason and connect ideas

Identify means name the feature. Name the crossing: bridge.

Describe means say what it is like. Six homes near it; two farther away.

Explain means give a reason and connect ideas. The crossing may make travel easier.

8–25 min · Teach the Geography

Identify means name

On screen: Give the requested feature. / Use the correct geographical term.

Command words tell us what kind of answer is needed. Identify means name or recognise. If the question asks us to identify the crossing, “footbridge” may be sufficient. A long story about why people need transport answers a different question. Point to the feature before naming it so pupils link the term to the visual. If several crossings are shown, add enough location information to distinguish the requested one. Accuracy comes before length: a short relevant answer can be better than a long unrelated one.

Brief check: Does “people travel faster” identify a crossing?
Listen for: No. It explains a possible effect rather than naming the feature.

Describe means say what it is like

On screen: Use position, shape and number. / Describe the visible pattern.

To describe a settlement, say where its buildings lie and how they are arranged. “Six homes are beside the bridge and two are farther away” gives a count and location. “People want jobs” is a possible explanation, not a description of the visible pattern. Move a finger across the image as you describe it so pupils can match each phrase to evidence. Useful description words include near, beside, north of, scattered and clustered. The relevant words depend on the feature being studied.

Brief check: Which adds detail: “some homes” or “six homes beside the bridge”?
Listen for: The second gives both number and location.

Explain means give the connection

On screen: Give a reason or process. / Show how it leads to the result.

An explanation needs more than the word because. “The homes are here because they are here” adds no cause. “A crossing may improve access, so people may choose nearby homes” supplies a mechanism. When the source shows only a pattern, use cautious language rather than pretending the cause was measured. Explain by tracing the sequence: crossing, easier access, possible location choice. The explanation should remain connected to the actual place or source in the question rather than becoming a memorised sentence about any settlement.

Brief check: What makes an explanation useful?
Listen for: It connects a reason or process to the result.

Answer the question asked

On screen: Find the command word. / Then find the place and evidence required.

Read a question in three parts: what to do, which feature or place, and which source to use. A pupil may know a correct fact but still fail to answer the question. Show a deliberate mismatch, such as a cause given when the question asks for a pattern. Repair the response by keeping any useful detail and replacing the irrelevant part. This is a method pupils can apply across Geography. A good answer is relevant, accurate and supported; its length depends on the task rather than on filling space.

Brief check: What should we check before adding more sentences?
Listen for: Whether the answer matches the command word and requested feature.

On screen: Look at a river flowing through a town. / An explanation needs the missing connection.

Look at a river flowing through a town. If the question says identify, name the feature: a river. If it says describe, give its visible characteristics: the channel bends beside buildings and passes under a bridge. If it says explain, connect a cause and an effect: the bridge lets people cross the river, linking roads on opposite banks. The subject stays the same; the job changes.

An explanation needs the missing connection. “There is a bridge” names a feature. “The bridge improves access because it joins the roads on both banks” explains a relationship. Match the answer to the command word before adding extra detail.

Words we will use

On screen: Claim: A statement to support or test / Evidence: Information supporting a claim / Reasoning: How evidence supports an answer

Claim means a statement to support or test. Most listed shops are near the stop.

Evidence means information supporting a claim. Twelve shops within 200 m; three farther away.

Reasoning means how evidence supports an answer. Access may help; the counts do not prove why.

8–25 min · Teach the Geography

Identify means name

On screen: Give the requested feature. / Use the correct geographical term.

Command words tell us what kind of answer is needed. Identify means name or recognise. If the question asks us to identify the crossing, “footbridge” may be sufficient. A long story about why people need transport answers a different question. Point to the feature before naming it so pupils link the term to the visual. If several crossings are shown, add enough location information to distinguish the requested one. Accuracy comes before length: a short relevant answer can be better than a long unrelated one.

Brief check: Does “people travel faster” identify a crossing?
Listen for: No. It explains a possible effect rather than naming the feature.

Describe means say what it is like

On screen: Use position, shape and number. / Describe the visible pattern.

To describe a settlement, say where its buildings lie and how they are arranged. “Six homes are beside the bridge and two are farther away” gives a count and location. “People want jobs” is a possible explanation, not a description of the visible pattern. Move a finger across the image as you describe it so pupils can match each phrase to evidence. Useful description words include near, beside, north of, scattered and clustered. The relevant words depend on the feature being studied.

Brief check: Which adds detail: “some homes” or “six homes beside the bridge”?
Listen for: The second gives both number and location.

Explain means give the connection

On screen: Give a reason or process. / Show how it leads to the result.

An explanation needs more than the word because. “The homes are here because they are here” adds no cause. “A crossing may improve access, so people may choose nearby homes” supplies a mechanism. When the source shows only a pattern, use cautious language rather than pretending the cause was measured. Explain by tracing the sequence: crossing, easier access, possible location choice. The explanation should remain connected to the actual place or source in the question rather than becoming a memorised sentence about any settlement.

Brief check: What makes an explanation useful?
Listen for: It connects a reason or process to the result.

Answer the question asked

On screen: Find the command word. / Then find the place and evidence required.

Read a question in three parts: what to do, which feature or place, and which source to use. A pupil may know a correct fact but still fail to answer the question. Show a deliberate mismatch, such as a cause given when the question asks for a pattern. Repair the response by keeping any useful detail and replacing the irrelevant part. This is a method pupils can apply across Geography. A good answer is relevant, accurate and supported; its length depends on the task rather than on filling space.

Brief check: What should we check before adding more sentences?
Listen for: Whether the answer matches the command word and requested feature.

Three questions about the same river

On screen: Look at a river flowing through a town. / An explanation needs the missing connection.

Look at a river flowing through a town. If the question says identify, name the feature: a river. If it says describe, give its visible characteristics: the channel bends beside buildings and passes under a bridge. If it says explain, connect a cause and an effect: the bridge lets people cross the river, linking roads on opposite banks. The subject stays the same; the job changes.

An explanation needs the missing connection. “There is a bridge” names a feature. “The bridge improves access because it joins the roads on both banks” explains a relationship. Match the answer to the command word before adding extra detail.

A claim needs support

On screen: Claim: what you say is true. / Evidence: the detail that supports it.

A claim states an idea about a place. Evidence is the observation, count or source detail we use to support that idea. “Shops cluster near the stop” is a claim. “Twelve of sixteen shops are within two hundred metres” makes the pattern more precise. Explain that evidence must be relevant: the colour of a shop sign does not test a claim about customer transport. We should be able to point to the supporting information and explain why it bears on the claim.

Brief check: Which supports clustering: a shop colour or a count with distance?
Listen for: The count and distance are relevant to the pattern.

Join evidence to the explanation

On screen: Say what the detail shows. / Explain why it matters.

A number does not explain itself. After giving a count, say what it tells us about the distribution. Then separate that pattern from a proposed cause. Many shops near a bus stop may be consistent with customers valuing access, but the count alone does not show why each business opened. Use two arrows: count to pattern, then possible access mechanism to explanation. The first can be directly supported by the count; the second needs more information about customers or business decisions.

Brief check: Can a location count tell us every business owner’s reason?
Listen for: No. It establishes the pattern, not every cause.

Ask for relevant new evidence

On screen: Customer survey: how did you travel? / Business records: when did the shop open?

The best next source depends on the claim being tested. If we want to know whether a bus stop brings customers, ask customers about travel and reasons for visiting. If we want to know whether the stop caused shops to open, compare opening dates and the stop’s history. Different questions need different evidence. More information is useful only if it addresses the uncertainty. Demonstrate a relevant and an irrelevant question, then explain why the relevant one could change our confidence in the proposed connection.

Brief check: Which evidence tests original opening: paint colour or dates?
Listen for: Dates can test whether the proposed cause came first.

State a useful limit

On screen: Say what is supported. / Say what still needs checking.

A limitation is a boundary on what we can conclude. It does not mean the investigation was worthless. We may accurately report that shops cluster in our mapped area while admitting that we did not measure the reasons for their location. Avoid extremes such as “we know everything” or “we know nothing”. Model a balanced conclusion: the source supports this pattern, a mechanism may explain it, and this further evidence would test that mechanism. Changing a claim when new evidence appears is part of good geographical reasoning.

Brief check: Does recognising a limit make all the evidence useless?
Listen for: No. Keep the supported finding and qualify the uncertain part.

Does a new bus stop improve access?

On screen: A proposal puts a bus stop outside a clinic. / Relevant evidence includes the timetable, distance to the entrance, step-free access and the locations of patients’ homes.

A proposal puts a bus stop outside a clinic. The claim is that this will improve access. The mechanism is plausible: some patients could travel by bus and walk a shorter distance to the entrance. But the sign alone cannot deliver the benefit. The service must run when patients need it, stop there and be usable by the people making the journey.

Relevant evidence includes the timetable, distance to the entrance, step-free access and the locations of patients’ homes. A photograph of the stop supports its existence, but cannot establish service frequency. A strong geographical explanation links the proposal, the people affected and evidence about the actual connection.

A count and distance support a geographical pattern.

A strong geographical explanation links the proposal, the people affected and evidence about the actual connection.

3–5 min · What this lesson explains

Compare matched evidence from two dates

On screen: Follow the map, diagram and explanation. / No copying is needed. The printed sheet is optional. / Ironbridge Gorge is in Shropshire, beside the River Severn. / Look at the same place on two dates. / A ferry crosses water in separate trips.

5–8 min · Make the words clear

Words we will use

On screen: Land use: How people use an area / Industry: Making goods and providing services / Change: A difference between two times

Land use means how people use an area. Fields can become housing.

Industry means making goods and providing services. Workshops make or repair goods.

Change means a difference between two times. A ferry crossing is replaced by a bridge.

Words we will use

On screen: Identify: Name the feature / Describe: Say what it is like / Explain: Give a reason and connect ideas

Identify means name the feature. Name the crossing: bridge.

Describe means say what it is like. Six homes near it; two farther away.

Explain means give a reason and connect ideas. The crossing may make travel easier.

Words we will use

On screen: Claim: A statement to support or test / Evidence: Information supporting a claim / Reasoning: How evidence supports an answer

Claim means a statement to support or test. Most listed shops are near the stop.

Evidence means information supporting a claim. Twelve shops within 200 m; three farther away.

Reasoning means how evidence supports an answer. Access may help; the counts do not prove why.

8–25 min · Reconnect and explain

Ironbridge Gorge: a changing industrial landscape

On screen: Ironbridge Gorge is in Shropshire, beside the River Severn. / Industry, transport and settlement changed the landscape.

Ironbridge Gorge is a real place in Shropshire associated with the Industrial Revolution. The River Severn runs through the gorge. Its historic industrial landscape includes evidence of manufacturing, transport and homes, while the iron bridge is an important example of early large-scale structural use of cast iron. Explain why this is more than a story about one bridge: industry changes land use, creates connections between workplaces and housing, and leaves material traces. Today, historical remains can also serve heritage and visitor purposes. Use this factual background to introduce change, while keeping our imagined before-and-after drawings separate from verified historical records. We can practise comparison with a schematic, but cannot use invented building counts to describe the actual gorge’s history.

Brief check: Why should the fictional drawing’s counts not become historical Ironbridge facts?
Listen for: They are classroom data rather than historical records.

Describe first, explain second

On screen: “A workshop appeared” describes change. / “Access may have helped” suggests a cause.

Descriptions tell us what differs between the sources. Explanations suggest why that difference occurred. A new workshop beside a bridge may lead us to ask whether improved access helped the business. Its location alone does not prove that cause. The workshop might have opened for another reason or before the bridge. Demonstrate both sentence types using the same image. Accurate description is the starting point; a causal explanation needs evidence linking the change in transport to the change in activity.

Brief check: Does being close to a bridge prove a business opened because of it?
Listen for: No. Location alone does not establish cause.

Test the proposed cause

On screen: A cause must come before its effect. / Use dates, records and comparisons.

If a shop opened in 2015 and the bridge opened in 2020, the bridge cannot explain the shop’s original opening. It could still affect later customer numbers. Split those two claims rather than accepting or rejecting everything at once. To investigate later effects, compare suitable records before and after the crossing, and consider other changes. This is how historical geography joins the story of a place to evidence. A convincing explanation identifies a possible mechanism and checks whether the timing and records support it.

Brief check: What does an earlier shop opening rule out?
Listen for: The later bridge cannot have caused that original opening.

What changes when a crossing opens?

On screen: Imagine two drawings of the same riverbank, five years apart. / The drawings alone do not prove that the bridge caused every new building.

Imagine two drawings of the same riverbank, five years apart. The earlier drawing shows a ferry landing and fields. The later one shows a bridge, a road and new shops. First describe the visible changes: transport infrastructure and land use have changed. Then suggest a connection: a permanent road crossing may make this bank easier to reach and attract customers.

The drawings alone do not prove that the bridge caused every new building. Planning decisions, population growth or another new road could also matter. Compare the dates of the changes and seek evidence about journeys and businesses. Keep this invented example separate from the real industrial history of Ironbridge Gorge.

The drawings alone do not prove that the bridge caused every new building. Planning decisions, population growth or another new road could also matter. Compare the dates of the changes and seek evidence about journeys and businesses. Keep this invented example separate from the real industrial history of Ironbridge Gorge.

Correction: The workshop appeared. Match the same feature across the two sources before describing change. A complete response must explain the method, not simply copy the correct choice. For a changed case, accept different answers only when the new condition actually supports them.

36–39 min · Brief spoken checks

What does an earlier shop opening rule out?

On screen: Think about the explanation. Answer aloud when invited.

If a shop opened in 2015 and the bridge opened in 2020, the bridge cannot explain the shop’s original opening. It could still affect later customer numbers. Split those two claims rather than accepting or rejecting everything at once. To investigate later effects, compare suitable records before and after the crossing, and consider other changes. This is how historical geography joins the story of a place to evidence. A convincing explanation identifies a possible mechanism and checks whether the timing and records support it.

Listen for this distinction: The later bridge cannot have caused that original opening.

What should we check before adding more sentences?

On screen: Think about the explanation. Answer aloud when invited.

Read a question in three parts: what to do, which feature or place, and which source to use. A pupil may know a correct fact but still fail to answer the question. Show a deliberate mismatch, such as a cause given when the question asks for a pattern. Repair the response by keeping any useful detail and replacing the irrelevant part. This is a method pupils can apply across Geography. A good answer is relevant, accurate and supported; its length depends on the task rather than on filling space.

On screen: Think about the explanation. Answer aloud when invited.

We may accurately report that shops cluster in our mapped area while admitting that we did not measure the reasons for their location. Avoid extremes such as “we know everything” or “we know nothing”. Changing a claim when new evidence appears is part of good geographical reasoning.

Does a new bus stop improve access?

On screen: Which supports clustering: a shop colour or a count with distance?

A proposal puts a bus stop outside a clinic. The claim is that this will improve access. The mechanism is plausible: some patients could travel by bus and walk a shorter distance to the entrance.

3–5 min · What this lesson explains

Replace certainty with a testable explanation

On screen: Follow the map, diagram and explanation. / No copying is needed. The printed sheet is optional. / Claim: what you say is true. / Say what the detail shows. / Customer survey: how did you travel?

This lesson explains how to support an explanation without overstating the evidence. The worked example shows the method, and the scheduled case shows how it applies to a different situation. Read the three geographical ideas aloud, then connect each one to a feature in the visual. Students can follow the demonstration without producing a written answer.

5–8 min · Make the words clear

Words we will use

On screen: Claim: A statement to support or test / Evidence: Information supporting a claim / Reasoning: How evidence supports an answer

Claim means a statement to support or test. Most listed shops are near the stop.

Evidence means information supporting a claim. Twelve shops within 200 m; three farther away.

Reasoning means how evidence supports an answer. Access may help; the counts do not prove why.

8–25 min · Teach the Geography

A claim needs support

On screen: Claim: what you say is true. / Evidence: the detail that supports it.

A claim states an idea about a place. Evidence is the observation, count or source detail we use to support that idea. “Shops cluster near the stop” is a claim. “Twelve of sixteen shops are within two hundred metres” makes the pattern more precise. Explain that evidence must be relevant: the colour of a shop sign does not test a claim about customer transport. We should be able to point to the supporting information and explain why it bears on the claim.

Brief check: Which supports clustering: a shop colour or a count with distance?
Listen for: The count and distance are relevant to the pattern.

Join evidence to the explanation

On screen: Say what the detail shows. / Explain why it matters.

A number does not explain itself. After giving a count, say what it tells us about the distribution. Then separate that pattern from a proposed cause. Many shops near a bus stop may be consistent with customers valuing access, but the count alone does not show why each business opened. Use two arrows: count to pattern, then possible access mechanism to explanation. The first can be directly supported by the count; the second needs more information about customers or business decisions.

Brief check: Can a location count tell us every business owner’s reason?
Listen for: No. It establishes the pattern, not every cause.

Ask for relevant new evidence

On screen: Customer survey: how did you travel? / Business records: when did the shop open?

The best next source depends on the claim being tested. If we want to know whether a bus stop brings customers, ask customers about travel and reasons for visiting. If we want to know whether the stop caused shops to open, compare opening dates and the stop’s history. Different questions need different evidence. More information is useful only if it addresses the uncertainty. Demonstrate a relevant and an irrelevant question, then explain why the relevant one could change our confidence in the proposed connection.

Brief check: Which evidence tests original opening: paint colour or dates?
Listen for: Dates can test whether the proposed cause came first.

State a useful limit

On screen: Say what is supported. / Say what still needs checking.

A limitation is a boundary on what we can conclude. It does not mean the investigation was worthless. We may accurately report that shops cluster in our mapped area while admitting that we did not measure the reasons for their location. Avoid extremes such as “we know everything” or “we know nothing”. Model a balanced conclusion: the source supports this pattern, a mechanism may explain it, and this further evidence would test that mechanism. Changing a claim when new evidence appears is part of good geographical reasoning.

Brief check: Does recognising a limit make all the evidence useless?
Listen for: No. Keep the supported finding and qualify the uncertain part.

Does a new bus stop improve access?

On screen: A proposal puts a bus stop outside a clinic. / Relevant evidence includes the timetable, distance to the entrance, step-free access and the locations of patients’ homes.

A proposal puts a bus stop outside a clinic. The claim is that this will improve access. The mechanism is plausible: some patients could travel by bus and walk a shorter distance to the entrance. But the sign alone cannot deliver the benefit. The service must run when patients need it, stop there and be usable by the people making the journey.

Relevant evidence includes the timetable, distance to the entrance, step-free access and the locations of patients’ homes. A photograph of the stop supports its existence, but cannot establish service frequency. A strong geographical explanation links the proposal, the people affected and evidence about the actual connection.

0–3 min · Introduce the geographical question

The shortest route may be unusable

On screen: Why might the straight line fail?

Two imagined routes lead from homes to a clinic. Route A is 400 metres but includes steps. Route B is 650 metres and step-free.

3–5 min · What this lesson explains

Evaluate a route for a named traveller

On screen: Follow the map, diagram and explanation. / No copying is needed. The printed sheet is optional. / Trace every section in order. / Stairs can be a barrier. / Constraint: a condition that must be met.

This lesson explains how to recommend a route for a named traveller. The worked example shows the method, and the scheduled case shows how it applies to a different situation. Read the three geographical ideas aloud, then connect each one to a feature in the visual. Students can follow the demonstration without producing a written answer.

Change the criteria when the user changes

On screen: Follow the map, diagram and explanation. / No copying is needed. The printed sheet is optional. / Trace every section in order. / Stairs can be a barrier. / Constraint: a condition that must be met.

This lesson explains how to recommend a route for a named traveller. The worked example shows the method, and the scheduled case shows how it applies to a different situation. Read the three geographical ideas aloud, then connect each one to a feature in the visual. Students can follow the demonstration without producing a written answer.

5–8 min · Make the words clear

Words we will use

On screen: Route: A path linking a start and destination / Constraint: A condition a plan must meet / Preference: Something a person would like

Route means a path linking a start and destination. School → library → market.

Constraint means a condition a plan must meet. A closed route cannot be used today.

Preference means something a person would like. A walker may prefer the shortest open route.

8–25 min · Teach the Geography

Routes connect a start and destination

On screen: Trace every section in order. / A straight line may not be a usable route.

A route is a sequence of connected sections between places. Trace the start, crossings, turns and destination. A straight line may be shorter on a map but could cross a fence, river or private land. The route must be usable by the traveller. Explain why geography considers the arrangement of places and the connections between them. Looking at distance alone ignores how the journey actually works. Before comparing routes, make sure each one begins and ends at the required locations and has no missing connection.

Brief check: Why might the straight line fail?
Listen for: It may cross a barrier or an inaccessible area.

Different travellers have different needs

On screen: Stairs can be a barrier. / Surface and slope affect access.

Imagine a traveller using a wheelchair and another walking without luggage. A staircase shortcut may work for one and prevent the other from travelling. A ramp label helps, but its gradient, width and surface condition still matter. Accessibility is a practical question about whether this person can use this route. It is not a judgement that one traveller is better than another. Point to the obstacle and explain its effect before comparing convenience. The shortest route may fail a necessary access condition.

Brief check: Should we choose stairs for every traveller because they are shorter?
Listen for: No. Check whether the traveller can use them.

Constraints and preferences

On screen: Constraint: a condition that must be met. / Preference: something we would like.

A constraint rules out a route when a required condition fails. A closed gate or unusable staircase can stop a journey. A preference helps choose between routes that work, such as a shorter distance or quieter surroundings. Establish feasibility before choosing favourites. Show a short closed route and a longer open route. The closed one cannot become feasible simply because we prefer it. This order makes a recommendation clear: first explain why the route can be used, then explain why it is the preferred usable option.

Brief check: Is an open route a preference or a necessary condition?
Listen for: Availability is a necessary condition.

Revise when conditions change

On screen: A closure can change the best route. / Check current conditions before travelling.

Maps describe locations and selected features, but they may not include a closure that happened this morning. A route that was suitable yesterday may be unavailable today. Show the old recommendation, add one changed condition and reconsider it aloud. Keep unchanged facts, such as the destination, while revising the affected route. Ask what information is needed before using an alternative: surface, crossing, opening hours or other relevant conditions. A good decision responds to evidence rather than defending an answer after its conditions have failed.

Brief check: What should happen to a recommendation after a route closes?
Listen for: Check alternatives and revise the route.

The shortest route may be unusable

On screen: Two imagined routes lead from homes to a clinic. / For a traveller able to use both, distance, lighting or traffic may influence the choice.

Two imagined routes lead from homes to a clinic. Route A is 400 metres but includes steps. Route B is 650 metres and step-free. For a traveller who cannot use steps, A fails an essential requirement even though it is shorter. A constraint determines whether a route is possible. A preference helps choose between possible routes.

For a traveller able to use both, distance, lighting or traffic may influence the choice. If B closes, the first task is to check whether another feasible route exists. Recommending the shortest line without checking access solves the wrong problem.

Access labels alone do not establish practical usability.

For a traveller able to use both, distance, lighting or traffic may influence the choice. If B closes, the first task is to check whether another feasible route exists. Recommending the shortest line without checking access solves the wrong problem.

Different priorities can justify different choices from the same evidence.
