0–3 min · Introduce the geographical question

The shortest route may be unusable

On screen: Why might the straight line fail?

Two imagined routes lead from homes to a clinic. Route A is 400 metres but includes steps. Route B is 650 metres and step-free.

Why a road map leaves things out

On screen: Is a satellite image automatically the same as a usable road map?

A driver needs roads, junctions and destinations. A walker may need footpaths, steep slopes and crossing points. A weather map may show rainfall without showing either network.

3–5 min · What this lesson explains

Treat availability as a constraint

On screen: Follow the map, diagram and explanation. / No copying is needed. The printed sheet is optional. / Trace every section in order. / Stairs can be a barrier. / Constraint: a condition that must be met.

This lesson explains how to recommend a route for a named traveller. The worked example shows the method, and the scheduled case shows how it applies to a different situation. Read the three geographical ideas aloud, then connect each one to a feature in the visual. Students can follow the demonstration without producing a written answer.

Select a map by its purpose and date

On screen: Follow the map, diagram and explanation. / No copying is needed. The printed sheet is optional. / Surveying improved position and distance information. / Maps select information. / Use the north arrow.

This lesson explains how to choose map information for a particular purpose. The worked example shows the method, and the scheduled case shows how it applies to a different situation. Read the three geographical ideas aloud, then connect each one to a feature in the visual. Students can follow the demonstration without producing a written answer.

5–8 min · Make the words clear

Words we will use

On screen: Route: A path linking a start and destination / Constraint: A condition a plan must meet / Preference: Something a person would like

Route means a path linking a start and destination. School → library → market.

Constraint means a condition a plan must meet. A closed route cannot be used today.

Preference means something a person would like. A walker may prefer the shortest open route.

Words we will use

On screen: Map: A selected view of an area / Survey: Measure and record an area / Layer: One type of information on a map

Map means a selected view of an area. A visitor map selects entrances and paths.

Survey means measure and record an area. Record lengths and locations of features.

Layer means one type of information on a map. A river layer differs from a boundary layer.

8–25 min · Teach the Geography

Routes connect a start and destination

On screen: Trace every section in order. / A straight line may not be a usable route.

A route is a sequence of connected sections between places. Trace the start, crossings, turns and destination. A straight line may be shorter on a map but could cross a fence, river or private land. The route must be usable by the traveller. Explain why geography considers the arrangement of places and the connections between them. Looking at distance alone ignores how the journey actually works. Before comparing routes, make sure each one begins and ends at the required locations and has no missing connection.

Brief check: Why might the straight line fail?
Listen for: It may cross a barrier or an inaccessible area.

Different travellers have different needs

On screen: Stairs can be a barrier. / Surface and slope affect access.

Imagine a traveller using a wheelchair and another walking without luggage. A staircase shortcut may work for one and prevent the other from travelling. A ramp label helps, but its gradient, width and surface condition still matter. Accessibility is a practical question about whether this person can use this route. It is not a judgement that one traveller is better than another. Point to the obstacle and explain its effect before comparing convenience. The shortest route may fail a necessary access condition.

Brief check: Should we choose stairs for every traveller because they are shorter?
Listen for: No. Check whether the traveller can use them.

Constraints and preferences

On screen: Constraint: a condition that must be met. / Preference: something we would like.

A constraint rules out a route when a required condition fails. A closed gate or unusable staircase can stop a journey. A preference helps choose between routes that work, such as a shorter distance or quieter surroundings. Establish feasibility before choosing favourites. Show a short closed route and a longer open route. The closed one cannot become feasible simply because we prefer it. This order makes a recommendation clear: first explain why the route can be used, then explain why it is the preferred usable option.

Brief check: Is an open route a preference or a necessary condition?
Listen for: Availability is a necessary condition.

Revise when conditions change

On screen: A closure can change the best route. / Check current conditions before travelling.

Maps describe locations and selected features, but they may not include a closure that happened this morning. A route that was suitable yesterday may be unavailable today. Show the old recommendation, add one changed condition and reconsider it aloud. Keep unchanged facts, such as the destination, while revising the affected route. Ask what information is needed before using an alternative: surface, crossing, opening hours or other relevant conditions. A good decision responds to evidence rather than defending an answer after its conditions have failed.

Brief check: What should happen to a recommendation after a route closes?
Listen for: Check alternatives and revise the route.

The shortest route may be unusable

On screen: Two imagined routes lead from homes to a clinic. / For a traveller able to use both, distance, lighting or traffic may influence the choice.

Two imagined routes lead from homes to a clinic. Route A is 400 metres but includes steps. Route B is 650 metres and step-free. For a traveller who cannot use steps, A fails an essential requirement even though it is shorter. A constraint determines whether a route is possible. A preference helps choose between possible routes.

For a traveller able to use both, distance, lighting or traffic may influence the choice. If B closes, the first task is to check whether another feasible route exists. Recommending the shortest line without checking access solves the wrong problem.

Map making has developed

On screen: Surveying improved position and distance information. / Digital maps combine data in changeable layers.

Maps have been made for navigation, ownership, government, exploration and many other purposes. Their development is not simply a move from bad pictures to good ones. Different maps serve different needs. Surveying methods improved the measurement of positions and distances; printing helped reproduce maps; aerial and satellite observations supplied further information. Digital systems can combine layers and update selected data. A satellite image is still not identical to a road map: it records visible information that must be interpreted and combined with other sources. Explain what each development makes possible, then keep the key questions unchanged: who made the map, for what purpose, at what date and scale? Technology can improve the information available without making every map complete or suitable for every journey.

Brief check: Is a satellite image automatically the same as a usable road map?
Listen for: No. A road map selects and explains information for a particular purpose.

A map has a purpose

On screen: Maps select information. / Different users need different detail.

A map represents selected information about a place. A road map helps drivers see routes; a historical map may show former buildings or industries; a weather map presents a different kind of information. No map can display every detail clearly at once. Ask who will use the map and which question it should answer. The omission of a feature may reflect the purpose or scale, rather than proving that the feature does not exist. Start by reading the title instead of treating every map as a complete picture.

Brief check: Does an absent symbol always prove a feature is absent on the ground?
Listen for: No. The map may omit it.

Direction needs a reference

On screen: Use the north arrow. / East and west are opposite directions.

On a north-up map, north is towards the top and east towards the right. However, a rotated map changes screen positions without changing real directions. Point to the north arrow first, then identify east, south and west relative to it. Use a route between two features to demonstrate a directional sentence. Direction describes one place relative to another, so reversing the journey can reverse the description. Do not use left and right as substitutes for compass directions unless the reference is clear.

Brief check: If we rotate a map, does the town move to a new real location?
Listen for: No. The view changes; the location does not.

A key translates symbols

On screen: Symbols simplify features. / The key explains their meanings.

A symbol stands for a feature so the map can be read without drawing every detail. A dot may mark a city, and a line may mark a road or river. Colours and shapes should be interpreted using the supplied key, not by assuming they always mean the same thing. Compare two possible keys for the same drawing. If a circle means a pond in one map and a town in another, the keys prevent confusion. Good map design keeps the meanings consistent within a map.

Brief check: Can we decide a symbol’s meaning from its colour alone?
Listen for: Use the key; colour alone may be ambiguous.

Check the date and scale

On screen: The date affects how current the map is. / The scale affects distance and detail.

A map may be excellent for one question and unsuitable for another. An old map can show past land use but may miss new roads. A small-scale regional map covers a broad area but may omit a local path. A large-scale map usually has more space for local detail. Date and scale therefore affect interpretation, alongside purpose. Demonstrate choosing a map for a local walking route and another for locating a country. The best map is the one whose information matches the geographical question.

Brief check: Which matters when checking a recently built road?
Listen for: The map’s date and whether it shows that level of detail.

Why a road map leaves things out

On screen: A driver needs roads, junctions and destinations. / Read the title, key, scale, direction and date.

A driver needs roads, junctions and destinations. A walker may need footpaths, steep slopes and crossing points. A weather map may show rainfall without showing either network. Each map selects information for a purpose. Leaving out individual trees on a road map is usually a sensible simplification, not evidence that the place has no trees.

Read the title, key, scale, direction and date. A blue line might mean a river on one map, but another key could use blue for a route. Digital layers change what is displayed without moving the real places. Choose information that answers the question.

25–32 min · Work through the examples

Worked example · 1.7

On screen: A closed path is not an option today even if its recorded length is shortest. / Cross unavailable choices out before ranking what remains.

A closed path is not an option today even if its recorded length is shortest. Cross unavailable choices out before ranking what remains. A recommendation needs both a route and the conditions under which it works.

A measured advantage cannot override an unavailable connection.

For a traveller able to use both, distance, lighting or traffic may influence the choice. If B closes, the first task is to check whether another feasible route exists. Recommending the shortest line without checking access solves the wrong problem.

Explain the contrast

On screen: The shorter bridge is closed. Which action comes first?

Response A: Find an open crossing before comparing journey lengths.

A measured advantage cannot override an unavailable connection.

Compare it with response B: Recommend it because it is still shortest.. The difference matters because for a traveller able to use both, distance, lighting or traffic may influence the choice. If B closes, the first task is to check whether another feasible route exists. Recommending the shortest line without checking access solves the wrong problem.

Worked example · 2.1

On screen: A factory map from the past can locate former industry; a current transport map can show bus connections. / Detail is selected for a purpose.

A factory map from the past can locate former industry; a current transport map can show bus connections. Detail is selected for a purpose. Older does not automatically mean useless.

Historical land use directly addresses former industry, though its date and coverage still matter.

Read the title, key, scale, direction and date. A blue line might mean a river on one map, but another key could use blue for a route. Digital layers change what is displayed without moving the real places. Choose information that answers the question.

Explain the contrast

On screen: Which map would best investigate former mills?

Response A: A dated historical land-use map.

Historical land use directly addresses former industry, though its date and coverage still matter.

Compare it with response B: Only today's bus timetable.. The difference matters because read the title, key, scale, direction and date. A blue line might mean a river on one map, but another key could use blue for a route. Digital layers change what is displayed without moving the real places. Choose information that answers the question.

32–36 min · Explain the scheduled case

Case explained · 1.7

On screen: Recommend open Route B; availability overrides the shorter measured distance.

Here is the case we are explaining. A new report says Route A is closed today. Route B remains open; distances are unchanged.

Recommend open Route B; availability overrides the shorter measured distance.

The geographical connection is this: For a traveller able to use both, distance, lighting or traffic may influence the choice. If B closes, the first task is to check whether another feasible route exists. Recommending the shortest line without checking access solves the wrong problem.

Change the example · 1.7

On screen: A is unavailable regardless of length. / Reconsider the open route or another open crossing.

Fictional routes: A is 500 m with stairs; B is 700 m with a ramp. Both are open. First traveller: a wheelchair user. Second traveller: a walker carrying a light bag. Ramp condition has not been checked.

The question is: New report: A is closed. What changes?

A is unavailable regardless of length. Reconsider the open route or another open crossing.

Case explained · 2.1

On screen: A helps investigate former mills; B helps plan current travel. / A may be outdated for travel; B may omit historical detail.

Here is the case we are explaining. Invented Map A (1900): river, bridge and mills. Map B (2026): roads, bus stops and public buildings.

A helps investigate former mills; B helps plan current travel. A may be outdated for travel; B may omit historical detail.

The geographical connection is this: Read the title, key, scale, direction and date. A blue line might mean a river on one map, but another key could use blue for a route. Digital layers change what is displayed without moving the real places. Choose information that answers the question.

Change the example · 2.1

On screen: For a journey: service times, disruption or step-free access. / Explain the user’s need.

Map A is a 1910 mill map. Map B is a current bus-route map with stops and connections, but no small paths. A visitor wants to investigate former industry, then travel by bus.

The question is: Name one useful piece of information missing from B.

For a journey: service times, disruption or step-free access. Explain the user’s need.

0–3 min · Introduce the geographical question

Make the scale do the work

On screen: Does one centimetre always represent twenty metres?

Our invented plan uses 1 centimetre to represent 20 metres. A building drawn 3 centimetres long represents 3 × 20 = 60 metres. To draw a 100-metre path at the same scale, reverse the operation: 100 ÷ 20 = 5 centimetres.

3–5 min · What this lesson explains

Convert real size into a scaled drawing

On screen: Follow the map, diagram and explanation. / No copying is needed. The printed sheet is optional. / 1 cm can represent many metres. / Measure the map line. / Choose the scale first.

This lesson explains how to draw and calculate using a map scale. The worked example shows the method, and the scheduled case shows how it applies to a different situation. Read the three geographical ideas aloud, then connect each one to a feature in the visual. Students can follow the demonstration without producing a written answer.

Diagnose a scale calculation rather than guess

On screen: Follow the map, diagram and explanation. / No copying is needed. The printed sheet is optional. / 1 cm can represent many metres. / Measure the map line. / Choose the scale first.

This lesson explains how to draw and calculate using a map scale. The worked example shows the method, and the scheduled case shows how it applies to a different situation. Read the three geographical ideas aloud, then connect each one to a feature in the visual. Students can follow the demonstration without producing a written answer.

5–8 min · Make the words clear

Words we will use

On screen: Plan: A view from directly above / Scale: The link between map and real distance / Symbol: A mark representing a feature

Plan means a view from directly above. A room drawn as if seen from the ceiling.

Scale means the link between map and real distance. At 1 cm = 2 m, an 8 m room is 4 cm long.

Symbol means a mark representing a feature. A drawn circle can represent a tree.

8–25 min · Teach the Geography

Scale connects the map to the ground

On screen: 1 cm can represent many metres. / Keep map units and ground units separate.

A map shrinks a place so it fits on a page or screen. Scale tells us how much ground distance is represented by a drawing distance. If one centimetre represents twenty metres, the centimetre belongs to the map and the metres belong to the ground. Show one centimetre, then two, then three equal sections. Their represented ground distances increase proportionally. Scale is a relationship, not an extra number to add to the measurement. Without it, a ruler tells us only the length of the drawing.

Brief check: Does one centimetre always represent twenty metres?
Listen for: No. It depends on the map’s scale.

From map distance to real distance

On screen: Measure the map line. / Multiply by the distance per centimetre.

At one centimetre to twenty metres, a five-centimetre path represents one hundred metres. Count five equal twenty-metre sections, then write five times twenty. Keep metres in the final answer. This concrete method shows why multiplication works before using a formula. If the line has several sections, add their map lengths before converting or convert each consistently and then add. Be careful not to measure a straight-line gap when the question asks for a route around obstacles.

Brief check: At 1 cm = 20 m, what does 2 cm represent?
Listen for: 40 m.

From ground distance to map distance

On screen: Choose the scale first. / Divide the ground distance by the scale value.

We can reverse the calculation when making a map. If one centimetre represents twenty metres, a hundred-metre boundary must be drawn as five centimetres. We divide one hundred by twenty to find how many map sections are needed. The unit of the answer is centimetres on the drawing. Check it by multiplying back to the original ground distance. A useful scale must also allow the whole area to fit on the page. A correct conversion that extends beyond the page is unsuitable for that drawing task.

Brief check: How can we check a reverse calculation?
Listen for: Multiply the map length by the scale and recover the ground distance.

Resizing changes the displayed scale

On screen: Enlarging doubles drawing lengths. / The actual ground distance stays the same.

Imagine enlarging a map to twice its original width and height. The places have not moved farther apart on the ground, but every drawn line is twice as long. The same real distance is now represented by more centimetres, so metres per displayed centimetre are smaller. A scale bar enlarged together with the map preserves its visual relationship; a printed ratio or statement must be interpreted for the new size. This is why measuring a projected picture with an ordinary ruler can be misleading.

Brief check: Does enlarging a map make the real journey longer?
Listen for: No. It changes the drawing, not the ground distance.

Make the scale do the work

On screen: Our invented plan uses 1 centimetre to represent 20 metres. / If the plan is enlarged to twice its printed width, the building becomes 6 centimetres long on the page but remains 60 metres long in reality.

Our invented plan uses 1 centimetre to represent 20 metres. A building drawn 3 centimetres long represents 3 × 20 = 60 metres. To draw a 100-metre path at the same scale, reverse the operation: 100 ÷ 20 = 5 centimetres. The map measurement and real distance describe the same length in different units and at different sizes.

If the plan is enlarged to twice its printed width, the building becomes 6 centimetres long on the page but remains 60 metres long in reality. The old written centimetre statement no longer fits. A scale bar enlarged with the map keeps the correct visual relationship.

Make the scale do the work

On screen: Our invented plan uses 1 centimetre to represent 20 metres. / If the plan is enlarged to twice its printed width, the building becomes 6 centimetres long on the page but remains 60 metres long in reality.

Our invented plan uses 1 centimetre to represent 20 metres. A building drawn 3 centimetres long represents 3 × 20 = 60 metres. To draw a 100-metre path at the same scale, reverse the operation: 100 ÷ 20 = 5 centimetres. The map measurement and real distance describe the same length in different units and at different sizes.

If the plan is enlarged to twice its printed width, the building becomes 6 centimetres long on the page but remains 60 metres long in reality. The old written centimetre statement no longer fits. A scale bar enlarged with the map keeps the correct visual relationship.

Mental maps are selective

On screen: We remember routes and landmarks. / Different people remember different features.

A mental map is a person’s remembered view of a place. It often includes familiar routes, important landmarks and destinations, while omitting unfamiliar areas. Two pupils can know the same neighbourhood but remember different features because they travel differently or value different places. A mental map can be useful without being perfectly measured. Explain its purpose: showing remembered relationships. Do not call every omission a mistake. The important question is whether the remembered information is sufficient and accurate for the task we want to perform.

Brief check: Why might two people’s remembered maps differ?
Listen for: Their experiences, routes and priorities can differ.

Landmarks help us navigate

On screen: A landmark is recognisable. / It helps us locate a turn or destination.

A useful landmark is something a traveller can recognise at the right point. “Turn beside the bridge” may be clearer than “turn after a while”. Follow a route using named landmarks in order. Explain how a landmark helps distinguish one junction from another. However, a shop sign can change and a small feature may be hard to see at night. Familiarity affects usefulness: a landmark obvious to one person may mean nothing to a visitor. A clear route description names features that the intended traveller can identify.

Brief check: What makes “after a while” a weak direction?
Listen for: It gives no clear landmark or measurable point.

Keep the route order

On screen: Start → landmark → turn → destination. / A missing step can break the journey.

Show a sequence of familiar places and trace it from the start. The order matters: the same landmarks in a different order may describe a different route. Include the direction of a turn where needed. Describe the journey aloud while moving a finger, then deliberately omit a step. Explain why the traveller would not know what to do at that point. A mental map is a provisional aid; important routes should be checked against current maps or direct observation when mistakes could prevent reaching the destination.

Brief check: Does a list of landmarks always give a usable route?
Listen for: No. Their sequence and connections must be clear.

Check memory against evidence

On screen: Compare remembered and mapped locations. / Update information that has changed.

Memory can distort distance and direction. A familiar walk may feel short, while an unfamiliar one feels longer even if their measured distances are similar. Compare a remembered route with a suitable map and identify a difference. Check whether the memory is inaccurate or the map is outdated. New construction, closures and changed landmarks can make old directions unsuitable. Updating a mental map is therefore an evidence task. Keep reliable remembered features while correcting the specific relationships that the comparison shows are wrong.

Brief check: Does a route feeling short establish its measured distance?
Listen for: No. Use suitable distance evidence.

A useful mental map can be incomplete

On screen: Imagine explaining the route from school to a shop: leave the gate, pass the park, turn right at the library and continue to the shop. / A familiar building may appear larger or closer in memory because it matters to you.

Imagine explaining the route from school to a shop: leave the gate, pass the park, turn right at the library and continue to the shop. This sequence can help a visitor even if you cannot remember the exact distances. A mental map selects landmarks and connections from experience rather than measuring every object.

A familiar building may appear larger or closer in memory because it matters to you. Keep the landmark order clear and mark uncertain turns or distances. Check important details against a reliable map or direct observation. Confidence is not a substitute for checking the route.

5–8 min · Make the words clear

Words we will use

On screen: Aerial view: A view from above / Key: An explanation of map symbols / Plan: A view from directly above

Aerial view means a view from above. An overhead photograph of school grounds.

Key means an explanation of map symbols. The key tells us which symbol means school.

Plan means a view from directly above. Simplify the view while keeping positions.

8–25 min · Teach the Geography

Aerial views look down

On screen: A photograph records visible detail. / A plan shows positions using simpler shapes.

An aerial view looks down towards the ground. It can reveal the arrangement of buildings, roads, vegetation and water more clearly than a view from street level. A photograph includes texture and shadows; a plan simplifies features into shapes and symbols. Point to one feature in the photograph and its matching position in the plan. We should preserve the important spatial relationships even when removing detail. A plan need not draw every roof tile to show where a building lies relative to a road.

Brief check: What should remain when detail is simplified?
Listen for: The relevant positions and spatial relationships.

Match features by their position

On screen: Use north, east, south and west. / Look for neighbouring features.

To translate an aerial view into a plan, identify a few stable features first. A pond west of a building should remain west of it in a north-up plan. Use neighbouring features as well as shape: a rectangular roof beside a playground can help identify a school. Camera angle and shadows may make appearances misleading, so avoid relying on one visual clue alone. Demonstrate matching the feature, locating it relative to others, and then replacing it with a simple symbol at the corresponding position.

Brief check: If north is up, where does a western feature belong?
Listen for: To the left of the reference feature.

Make a consistent key

On screen: One symbol has one meaning. / Use distinct symbols for different features.

A key is a translation between map symbols and real features. A blue circle for a pond and a rectangle for a building can work if their meanings are explained. If the plan uses the same symbol for different features without explanation, readers may confuse them. Show a deliberately mismatched key and correct either the symbol or the label so they agree. The task is consistency, not choosing one universally perfect symbol. Symbols should also be readable at the size in which the map will be used.

Brief check: What is wrong if the key says pond but the symbol marks a school?
Listen for: The symbol and key do not match.

Simplification has limits

On screen: A plan can show arrangement. / It may not show height or current use.

A simple plan can show where features are, but may not reveal how tall a building is or what happens inside it. An aerial photograph can show a roof without proving the building’s current purpose. Explain what each source directly provides and what needs another source. A simplified school plan may be excellent for finding the library but unsuitable for assessing a steep path unless height or slope information is included. Good geographical interpretation chooses the source that measures the property in the question.

Brief check: Does a roof shape prove what a building is used for today?
Listen for: No. Its use needs other evidence.

On screen: In our imaginary school site, the school is west, a pond is east, a road is south and a park is north. / Add a north arrow and a key that explains every symbol.

In our imaginary school site, the school is west, a pond is east, a road is south and a park is north. A plan looks straight down. Replace detailed objects with simple consistent symbols while preserving these relative positions. The pond remains east of the school even when its shape is simplified.

Add a north arrow and a key that explains every symbol. A blue patch means water only if the key makes that meaning clear. A plan can omit detail for readability, but should retain what its user needs, such as the entrance beside the southern road.

Make the scale do the work

On screen: Does one centimetre always represent twenty metres?

5–8 min · Make the words clear

Words we will use

On screen: Plan: A view from directly above / Scale: The link between map and real distance / Symbol: A mark representing a feature

Plan means a view from directly above. A room drawn as if seen from the ceiling.

Scale means the link between map and real distance. At 1 cm = 2 m, an 8 m room is 4 cm long.

Symbol means a mark representing a feature. A drawn circle can represent a tree.

Words we will use

On screen: Mental map: A place represented from memory / Landmark: A recognisable feature / Route: A path between places

Mental map means a place represented from memory. Draw the landmarks you remember.

Landmark means a recognisable feature. The library helps a visitor recognise a turn.

Route means a path between places. School → park → library → bridge.

Words we will use

On screen: Aerial view: A view from above / Key: An explanation of map symbols / Plan: A view from directly above

Aerial view means a view from above. An overhead photograph of school grounds.

Key means an explanation of map symbols. The key tells us which symbol means school.

Plan means a view from directly above. Simplify the view while keeping positions.

8–25 min · Reconnect and explain

Scale connects the map to the ground

On screen: 1 cm can represent many metres. / Keep map units and ground units separate.

A map shrinks a place so it fits on a page or screen. Scale tells us how much ground distance is represented by a drawing distance. If one centimetre represents twenty metres, the centimetre belongs to the map and the metres belong to the ground. Show one centimetre, then two, then three equal sections. Their represented ground distances increase proportionally. Scale is a relationship, not an extra number to add to the measurement. Without it, a ruler tells us only the length of the drawing.

Brief check: Does one centimetre always represent twenty metres?
Listen for: No. It depends on the map’s scale.

From ground distance to map distance

On screen: Choose the scale first. / Divide the ground distance by the scale value.

We can reverse the calculation when making a map. If one centimetre represents twenty metres, a hundred-metre boundary must be drawn as five centimetres. We divide one hundred by twenty to find how many map sections are needed. The unit of the answer is centimetres on the drawing. Check it by multiplying back to the original ground distance. A useful scale must also allow the whole area to fit on the page. A correct conversion that extends beyond the page is unsuitable for that drawing task.

Brief check: How can we check a reverse calculation?
Listen for: Multiply the map length by the scale and recover the ground distance.

Resizing changes the displayed scale

On screen: Enlarging doubles drawing lengths. / The actual ground distance stays the same.

Imagine enlarging a map to twice its original width and height. The places have not moved farther apart on the ground, but every drawn line is twice as long. The same real distance is now represented by more centimetres, so metres per displayed centimetre are smaller. A scale bar enlarged together with the map preserves its visual relationship; a printed ratio or statement must be interpreted for the new size. This is why measuring a projected picture with an ordinary ruler can be misleading.

Brief check: Does enlarging a map make the real journey longer?
Listen for: No. It changes the drawing, not the ground distance.

Make the scale do the work

On screen: Our invented plan uses 1 centimetre to represent 20 metres. / If the plan is enlarged to twice its printed width, the building becomes 6 centimetres long on the page but remains 60 metres long in reality.

Our invented plan uses 1 centimetre to represent 20 metres. A building drawn 3 centimetres long represents 3 × 20 = 60 metres. To draw a 100-metre path at the same scale, reverse the operation: 100 ÷ 20 = 5 centimetres. The map measurement and real distance describe the same length in different units and at different sizes.

If the plan is enlarged to twice its printed width, the building becomes 6 centimetres long on the page but remains 60 metres long in reality. The old written centimetre statement no longer fits. A scale bar enlarged with the map keeps the correct visual relationship.

Mental maps are selective

On screen: We remember routes and landmarks. / Different people remember different features.

A mental map is a person’s remembered view of a place. It often includes familiar routes, important landmarks and destinations, while omitting unfamiliar areas. Two pupils can know the same neighbourhood but remember different features because they travel differently or value different places. A mental map can be useful without being perfectly measured. Explain its purpose: showing remembered relationships. Do not call every omission a mistake. The important question is whether the remembered information is sufficient and accurate for the task we want to perform.

Brief check: Why might two people’s remembered maps differ?
Listen for: Their experiences, routes and priorities can differ.

Keep the route order

On screen: Start → landmark → turn → destination. / A missing step can break the journey.

Show a sequence of familiar places and trace it from the start. The order matters: the same landmarks in a different order may describe a different route. Include the direction of a turn where needed. Describe the journey aloud while moving a finger, then deliberately omit a step. Explain why the traveller would not know what to do at that point. A mental map is a provisional aid; important routes should be checked against current maps or direct observation when mistakes could prevent reaching the destination.

Brief check: Does a list of landmarks always give a usable route?
Listen for: No. Their sequence and connections must be clear.

Keep reliable remembered features while correcting the specific relationships that the comparison shows are wrong.

Listen for: No. Use suitable distance evidence.

Class board challenge · Diagnose a scale calculation rather than guess

On screen: Follow the teacher’s demonstration on the map.

36–39 min · Brief spoken checks

Does enlarging a map make the real journey longer?

On screen: Think about the explanation. Answer aloud when invited.

Imagine enlarging a map to twice its original width and height. The places have not moved farther apart on the ground, but every drawn line is twice as long. The same real distance is now represented by more centimetres, so metres per displayed centimetre are smaller. A scale bar enlarged together with the map preserves its visual relationship; a printed ratio or statement must be interpreted for the new size. This is why measuring a projected picture with an ordinary ruler can be misleading.

Listen for this distinction: No. It changes the drawing, not the ground distance.

Does a route feeling short establish its measured distance?

On screen: Think about the explanation. Answer aloud when invited.

Memory can distort distance and direction. A familiar walk may feel short, while an unfamiliar one feels longer even if their measured distances are similar. Compare a remembered route with a suitable map and identify a difference. Check whether the memory is inaccurate or the map is outdated. New construction, closures and changed landmarks can make old directions unsuitable. Updating a mental map is therefore an evidence task. Keep reliable remembered features while correcting the specific relationships that the comparison shows are wrong.

Listen for this distinction: No. Use suitable distance evidence.

Does a roof shape prove what a building is used for today?

On screen: Think about the explanation. Answer aloud when invited.

A simple plan can show where features are, but may not reveal how tall a building is or what happens inside it. An aerial photograph can show a roof without proving the building’s current purpose. Explain what each source directly provides and what needs another source. A simplified school plan may be excellent for finding the library but unsuitable for assessing a steep path unless height or slope information is included. Good geographical interpretation chooses the source that measures the property in the question.

Listen for this distinction: No. Its use needs other evidence.

0–3 min · Introduce the geographical question

Turn the scene into a plan

On screen: What should remain when detail is simplified?

In our imaginary school site, the school is west, a pond is east, a road is south and a park is north. A plan looks straight down. Replace detailed objects with simple consistent symbols while preserving these relative positions.

Across before up

On screen: Which do we read first?

A grid square begins at easting 23 and northing 45. Read across to its left edge, then up to its bottom edge: the four-figure reference is 2345. That reference identifies the whole square.

3–5 min · What this lesson explains

Select map detail for a specific journey

On screen: Follow the map, diagram and explanation. / No copying is needed. The printed sheet is optional. / A photograph records visible detail. / Use north, east, south and west. / One symbol has one meaning.

This lesson explains how to turn a view from above into a clear plan. The worked example shows the method, and the scheduled case shows how it applies to a different situation. Read the three geographical ideas aloud, then connect each one to a feature in the visual. Students can follow the demonstration without producing a written answer.

Read a grid square before adding tenths

On screen: Follow the map, diagram and explanation. / No copying is needed. The printed sheet is optional. / Eastings go across. / Use the square’s left easting. / Divide the square into ten parts across.

This lesson explains how to locate squares and points using grid references. The worked example shows the method, and the scheduled case shows how it applies to a different situation. Read the three geographical ideas aloud, then connect each one to a feature in the visual. Students can follow the demonstration without producing a written answer.

5–8 min · Make the words clear

Words we will use

On screen: Aerial view: A view from above / Key: An explanation of map symbols / Plan: A view from directly above

Aerial view means a view from above. An overhead photograph of school grounds.

Key means an explanation of map symbols. The key tells us which symbol means school.

Plan means a view from directly above. Simplify the view while keeping positions.

Words we will use

On screen: Easting: A numbered line read across the map / Northing: A numbered line read up the map / Grid reference: Numbers locating a square or point

Easting means a numbered line read across the map. Read across to easting 23.

Northing means a numbered line read up the map. Read up to northing 45.

Grid reference means numbers locating a square or point. Square 2345; add tenths for a precise point.

8–25 min · Teach the Geography

Aerial views look down

On screen: A photograph records visible detail. / A plan shows positions using simpler shapes.

An aerial view looks down towards the ground. It can reveal the arrangement of buildings, roads, vegetation and water more clearly than a view from street level. A photograph includes texture and shadows; a plan simplifies features into shapes and symbols. Point to one feature in the photograph and its matching position in the plan. We should preserve the important spatial relationships even when removing detail. A plan need not draw every roof tile to show where a building lies relative to a road.

Brief check: What should remain when detail is simplified?
Listen for: The relevant positions and spatial relationships.

Match features by their position

On screen: Use north, east, south and west. / Look for neighbouring features.

To translate an aerial view into a plan, identify a few stable features first. A pond west of a building should remain west of it in a north-up plan. Use neighbouring features as well as shape: a rectangular roof beside a playground can help identify a school. Camera angle and shadows may make appearances misleading, so avoid relying on one visual clue alone. Demonstrate matching the feature, locating it relative to others, and then replacing it with a simple symbol at the corresponding position.

Brief check: If north is up, where does a western feature belong?
Listen for: To the left of the reference feature.

Make a consistent key

On screen: One symbol has one meaning. / Use distinct symbols for different features.

A key is a translation between map symbols and real features. A blue circle for a pond and a rectangle for a building can work if their meanings are explained. If the plan uses the same symbol for different features without explanation, readers may confuse them. Show a deliberately mismatched key and correct either the symbol or the label so they agree. The task is consistency, not choosing one universally perfect symbol. Symbols should also be readable at the size in which the map will be used.

Brief check: What is wrong if the key says pond but the symbol marks a school?
Listen for: The symbol and key do not match.

Simplification has limits

On screen: A plan can show arrangement. / It may not show height or current use.

A simple plan can show where features are, but may not reveal how tall a building is or what happens inside it. An aerial photograph can show a roof without proving the building’s current purpose. Explain what each source directly provides and what needs another source. A simplified school plan may be excellent for finding the library but unsuitable for assessing a steep path unless height or slope information is included. Good geographical interpretation chooses the source that measures the property in the question.

Brief check: Does a roof shape prove what a building is used for today?
Listen for: No. Its use needs other evidence.

Turn the scene into a plan

On screen: In our imaginary school site, the school is west, a pond is east, a road is south and a park is north. / Add a north arrow and a key that explains every symbol.

In our imaginary school site, the school is west, a pond is east, a road is south and a park is north. A plan looks straight down. Replace detailed objects with simple consistent symbols while preserving these relative positions. The pond remains east of the school even when its shape is simplified.

Add a north arrow and a key that explains every symbol. A blue patch means water only if the key makes that meaning clear. A plan can omit detail for readability, but should retain what its user needs, such as the entrance beside the southern road.

A grid gives a shared location system

On screen: Eastings go across. / Northings go up.

Grid lines provide a common way to locate places on a map. Easting numbers increase towards the east; northing numbers increase towards the north. Always read eastings first. Trace across the map before moving up and say the order aloud. A reference is meaningful within its map or grid system, so it should not be treated as an address that works everywhere. On Ordnance Survey maps, the National Grid also uses a letter prefix to identify the larger grid area. Our exercise uses a small practice grid.

Brief check: Which do we read first?
Listen for: Eastings first, then northings.

Four figures identify a square

On screen: Use the square’s left easting. / Then use its bottom northing.

A four-figure reference identifies a grid square, rather than one exact point. Locate the left boundary of the square and read its easting. Locate the bottom boundary and read its northing. Join these two two-digit values in that order. For practice square 2345, twenty-three is the left easting and forty-five the bottom northing. Do not use the nearest line without checking which boundary it represents. Several features can share the same four-figure square, which explains why more detail may be needed.

Brief check: Does 2345 identify just one building?
Listen for: No. It identifies a square that may contain several features.

Six figures add tenths

On screen: Divide the square into ten parts across. / Then divide it into ten parts up.

To locate a point more precisely, estimate tenths within the square. Add the across tenth to the easting half, then add the upward tenth to the northing half. In square 2345, a point six tenths across and two tenths up becomes 236452. Build the two halves separately: two-three-six, then four-five-two. This reduces the risk of putting both tenths at the end. On a one-kilometre National Grid square, a six-figure reference identifies a one-hundred-metre square rather than a perfectly exact mathematical point.

Brief check: What changes when only the easting tenth increases?
Listen for: The location moves east within the practice square.

Check by plotting back

On screen: Read the two halves separately. / Plot the result and compare with the target.

A reference should lead another reader back to the intended location. Split the six figures into easting and northing halves, identify the square, then position the tenths. If the point appears in the wrong part of the square, check whether the tenths were swapped or the order reversed. Show the original target beside a wrongly plotted point. A valid-looking string of six digits is not enough: it must match the intended place. Plotting back checks the meaning of the answer rather than just its format.

Brief check: Why is plotting back useful?
Listen for: It tests whether the reference actually identifies the intended location.

Across before up

On screen: A grid square begins at easting 23 and northing 45. / A point six tenths across and two tenths up gives easting 236 and northing 452, combined as 236452.

A grid square begins at easting 23 and northing 45. Read across to its left edge, then up to its bottom edge: the four-figure reference is 2345. That reference identifies the whole square. To locate a point more precisely, divide the square mentally into ten equal parts in each direction.

A point six tenths across and two tenths up gives easting 236 and northing 452, combined as 236452. The first three digits go together; the last three go together. Check by plotting the reference back into the square. Reversing the groups sends the reader to a different location.

7A · Week 31 · sections 2.6, 2.6

40-minute planning estimate: introduction 3, goal 2, vocabulary 3, explanation 17, worked examples 7, case explanation 4, spoken checks 3, recap 1. Divide each block between topics in combined lessons. Adjust to the class; elapsed classroom teaching time has not been measured.

0–3 min · Introduce the geographical question

A straight line cannot walk around a wall

On screen: Which distance includes the detour around a fence?

On an invented map, the direct line between a gate and a library is 4 centimetres. The usable path has three sections: 2, 3 and 1 centimetres. At 1 centimetre to 100 metres, the direct distance is 400 metres, but the walked route is (2 + 3 + 1) × 100 = 600 metres.

3–5 min · What this lesson explains

Measure the route rather than the straight-line gap

On screen: Follow the map, diagram and explanation. / No copying is needed. The printed sheet is optional. / Direct distance joins start and finish. / Measure each section once. / Convert both routes with their map scales.

This lesson explains how to measure and compare routes using scale. The worked example shows the method, and the scheduled case shows how it applies to a different situation. Read the three geographical ideas aloud, then connect each one to a feature in the visual. Students can follow the demonstration without producing a written answer.

Compare like with like when selecting a route

On screen: Follow the map, diagram and explanation. / No copying is needed. The printed sheet is optional. / Direct distance joins start and finish. / Measure each section once. / Convert both routes with their map scales.

This lesson explains how to measure and compare routes using scale. The worked example shows the method, and the scheduled case shows how it applies to a different situation. Read the three geographical ideas aloud, then connect each one to a feature in the visual. Students can follow the demonstration without producing a written answer.

5–8 min · Make the words clear

Words we will use

On screen: Scale: The link between map and real distance / Distance: How far apart places are / Unit: A measurement such as metres

Scale means the link between map and real distance. At 1 cm = 100 m, 4 cm represents 400 m.

Distance means how far apart places are. Add every section of the walking route.

Unit means a measurement such as metres. 400 m, not an unexplained “400”.

8–25 min · Teach the Geography

Direct distance and route distance

On screen: Direct distance joins start and finish. / Route distance follows the usable path.

Direct distance is the straight-line separation between two places. Route distance follows the actual journey, including bends and detours. A river or fence can make the route longer than the direct line. Show both on the same drawing and trace each separately. Before measuring, decide which distance the question asks for. The shortest visible line is not automatically a usable route. Geography uses distance alongside connections and barriers to explain why places that look close together can take longer to reach.

Brief check: Which distance includes the detour around a fence?
Listen for: Route distance.

Add all route sections

On screen: Measure each section once. / Use the same unit throughout.

A route made of several straight sections can be measured section by section. Label each length so no section is missed or counted twice. Add map lengths in the same unit before converting with the scale. If the route has two, three and one centimetre sections, its map length is six centimetres. Explain why we do not include the direct gap as another section. It is a different measurement of the same start and destination. Keep the route visibly highlighted while building the addition.

Brief check: Do we add the direct gap to the route sections?
Listen for: No. The direct gap is not an extra travelled section.

Use scale to compare fairly

On screen: Convert both routes with their map scales. / Compare ground distances in the same unit.

A drawn line is not a real distance until we apply its map scale. Two routes on the same map can be compared using the same metres-per-centimetre relationship. If they are on different maps, their scales may differ, so compare their converted ground distances rather than drawing lengths. Change metres to kilometres consistently when necessary. A shorter drawn route can represent a longer real route if its map covers much more ground per centimetre. The scale is part of the evidence, not a detail to ignore.

Brief check: Can we compare centimetres from two different scales directly?
Listen for: No. Convert to comparable ground distances first.

Distance is one part of a recommendation

On screen: Check access and closures. / Then compare time or convenience.

A route recommendation needs the traveller’s needs and current conditions as well as distance. A shorter route may include stairs or a closed crossing. A longer one may be the only feasible route. Explain the sequence: confirm the route connects the required places, check that it can be used, then compare distance or other preferences. Do not assume a map shows today’s service status. A careful recommendation states the condition on which it depends and names one relevant check before a real journey.

Brief check: What could make the shorter route unsuitable?
Listen for: A barrier, closure or access problem for the traveller.

A straight line cannot walk around a wall

On screen: On an invented map, the direct line between a gate and a library is 4 centimetres. / The direct line measures separation; the route measures the path followed.

On an invented map, the direct line between a gate and a library is 4 centimetres. The usable path has three sections: 2, 3 and 1 centimetres. At 1 centimetre to 100 metres, the direct distance is 400 metres, but the walked route is (2 + 3 + 1) × 100 = 600 metres. The route is 200 metres longer.

The direct line measures separation; the route measures the path followed. A river, wall or closed entrance can make the direct line unusable. Add every section before converting, then check units and access. Neither distance alone establishes a journey time without a suitable walking speed.

The direct line measures separation; the route measures the path followed. A river, wall or closed entrance can make the direct line unusable. Add every section before converting, then check units and access. Neither distance alone establishes a journey time without a suitable walking speed.

Key means an explanation of map symbols. A practice key may show P for parking.

Grid reference means numbers locating a square or point. Eastings before northings.

Brief check: Can we compare centimetres from two different scales directly?
Listen for: No. Convert to comparable ground distances first.

Distance is one part of a recommendation

On screen: Check access and closures. / Then compare time or convenience.

A route recommendation needs the traveller’s needs and current conditions as well as distance. A shorter route may include stairs or a closed crossing. A longer one may be the only feasible route. Explain the sequence: confirm the route connects the required places, check that it can be used, then compare distance or other preferences. Do not assume a map shows today’s service status. A careful recommendation states the condition on which it depends and names one relevant check before a real journey.

Brief check: What could make the shorter route unsuitable?
Listen for: A barrier, closure or access problem for the traveller.

A straight line cannot walk around a wall

On screen: On an invented map, the direct line between a gate and a library is 4 centimetres. / The direct line measures separation; the route measures the path followed.

On an invented map, the direct line between a gate and a library is 4 centimetres. The usable path has three sections: 2, 3 and 1 centimetres. At 1 centimetre to 100 metres, the direct distance is 400 metres, but the walked route is (2 + 3 + 1) × 100 = 600 metres. The route is 200 metres longer.

The direct line measures separation; the route measures the path followed. A river, wall or closed entrance can make the direct line unusable. Add every section before converting, then check units and access. Neither distance alone establishes a journey time without a suitable walking speed.

Read an OS map’s information

On screen: Read the legend and symbols. / Check scale and grid information.

Ordnance Survey maps use symbols, a National Grid and scales to describe places in Great Britain. Begin with the map information rather than guessing from an isolated symbol. The legend explains the features shown, and the grid supports location references. A map designed for walking needs different detail from a broad regional map. Our classroom diagrams practise the skills but are not reproduced official map extracts. Explain that a real map’s edition and current conditions also matter when planning an outdoor route.

Brief check: What should we consult to decode an unfamiliar symbol?
Listen for: The map’s legend or key.

A ratio scale uses the same units

On screen: 1:25,000 means 1 unit to 25,000 units. / 1 cm represents 250 m.

A ratio scale compares like units. At one to twenty-five thousand, one centimetre on the map represents twenty-five thousand centimetres on the ground. Convert those ground centimetres to metres by dividing by one hundred: the result is two hundred and fifty metres. Write the conversion as a sequence rather than skipping the units. A pupil who reports twenty-five thousand metres has retained the number but changed the unit incorrectly. The ratio itself does not require centimetres, but both sides must use the same unit before conversion.

Brief check: Why is 25,000 cm not 25,000 m?
Listen for: A metre contains one hundred centimetres.

Coverage and detail change with scale

On screen: 1:25,000 usually shows more local detail. / 1:250,000 covers more ground in the same space.

At one to two hundred and fifty thousand, each map centimetre represents two thousand five hundred metres. That is ten times the ground distance represented at one to twenty-five thousand. The broader-scale map fits more territory on a page but has less room for small features. The smaller denominator is called the larger scale. Explain the relationship with the ground distance rather than expecting pupils to memorise the terminology alone. Choose a scale according to whether we need local walking detail or a broad overview.

Brief check: Which gives more page space to one kilometre?
Listen for: The 1:25,000 map.

Symbols do not guarantee access

On screen: An intersection may need a crossing. / Current access needs a separate check.

A footpath line crossing a stream line raises a practical question: how does the traveller cross? Look for the relevant crossing information, but do not assume that every intersection is a safe bridge. Map symbols provide evidence about selected features at the map’s date; they do not guarantee present safety or permission. Conditions can change after publication. Model a route decision that uses scale, symbols and a clearly stated check. This joins map reading to sensible interpretation without turning a classroom drawing into live travel advice.

Brief check: Does two crossing lines automatically mean a safe bridge?
Listen for: No. Check the crossing information and current conditions.

A map symbol is information with conditions

On screen: A topographic map can show a track, a wooded area and contour lines near a village. / At 1:25,000, one centimetre represents 25,000 centimetres, or 250 metres.

A topographic map can show a track, a wooded area and contour lines near a village. Its key tells us what the symbols represent. A track symbol establishes that a mapped track exists; it does not automatically establish public permission, safe conditions or an open gate today. Use the information for the question it actually answers.

At 1:25,000, one centimetre represents 25,000 centimetres, or 250 metres. At 1:50,000 it represents 500 metres. At the same paper size, 1:25,000 usually offers more local detail over a smaller area. A larger denominator does not mean a larger-scale map.

At the same paper size, 1:25,000 usually offers more local detail over a smaller area. A larger denominator does not mean a larger-scale map.

The direct line measures separation; the route measures the path followed. A river, wall or closed entrance can make the direct line unusable. Add every section before converting, then check units and access. Neither distance alone establishes a journey time without a suitable walking speed.

A careful recommendation states the condition on which it depends and names one relevant check before a real journey.

0–3 min · Introduce the geographical question

A map symbol is information with conditions

On screen: What should we consult to decode an unfamiliar symbol?

A topographic map can show a track, a wooded area and contour lines near a village. Its key tells us what the symbols represent. A track symbol establishes that a mapped track exists; it does not automatically establish public permission, safe conditions or an open gate today.

5–8 min · Make the words clear

Words we will use

On screen: Ordnance Survey: Britain’s national mapping agency / Key: An explanation of map symbols / Grid reference: Numbers locating a square or point

Ordnance Survey means britain’s national mapping agency. Use the map’s own official key.

Key means an explanation of map symbols. A practice key may show P for parking.

Grid reference means numbers locating a square or point. Eastings before northings.

Words we will use

On screen: Contour: A line joining equal heights / Relief: The shape and height of the land / Gradient: How steep a slope is

Contour means a line joining equal heights. Points on one contour have equal height.

Relief means the shape and height of the land. Show low ground, hills and valleys.

Gradient means how steep a slope is. Compare rise with horizontal distance.

8–25 min · Teach the Geography

Read an OS map’s information

On screen: Read the legend and symbols. / Check scale and grid information.

Ordnance Survey maps use symbols, a National Grid and scales to describe places in Great Britain. Begin with the map information rather than guessing from an isolated symbol. The legend explains the features shown, and the grid supports location references. A map designed for walking needs different detail from a broad regional map. Our classroom diagrams practise the skills but are not reproduced official map extracts. Explain that a real map’s edition and current conditions also matter when planning an outdoor route.

Brief check: What should we consult to decode an unfamiliar symbol?
Listen for: The map’s legend or key.

A ratio scale uses the same units

On screen: 1:25,000 means 1 unit to 25,000 units. / 1 cm represents 250 m.

A ratio scale compares like units. At one to twenty-five thousand, one centimetre on the map represents twenty-five thousand centimetres on the ground. Convert those ground centimetres to metres by dividing by one hundred: the result is two hundred and fifty metres. Write the conversion as a sequence rather than skipping the units. A pupil who reports twenty-five thousand metres has retained the number but changed the unit incorrectly. The ratio itself does not require centimetres, but both sides must use the same unit before conversion.

Brief check: Why is 25,000 cm not 25,000 m?
Listen for: A metre contains one hundred centimetres.

Coverage and detail change with scale

On screen: 1:25,000 usually shows more local detail. / 1:250,000 covers more ground in the same space.

At one to two hundred and fifty thousand, each map centimetre represents two thousand five hundred metres. That is ten times the ground distance represented at one to twenty-five thousand. The broader-scale map fits more territory on a page but has less room for small features. The smaller denominator is called the larger scale. Explain the relationship with the ground distance rather than expecting pupils to memorise the terminology alone. Choose a scale according to whether we need local walking detail or a broad overview.

Brief check: Which gives more page space to one kilometre?
Listen for: The 1:25,000 map.

Symbols do not guarantee access

On screen: An intersection may need a crossing. / Current access needs a separate check.

A footpath line crossing a stream line raises a practical question: how does the traveller cross? Look for the relevant crossing information, but do not assume that every intersection is a safe bridge. Map symbols provide evidence about selected features at the map’s date; they do not guarantee present safety or permission. Conditions can change after publication. Model a route decision that uses scale, symbols and a clearly stated check. This joins map reading to sensible interpretation without turning a classroom drawing into live travel advice.

Brief check: Does two crossing lines automatically mean a safe bridge?
Listen for: No. Check the crossing information and current conditions.

A map symbol is information with conditions

On screen: A topographic map can show a track, a wooded area and contour lines near a village. / At 1:25,000, one centimetre represents 25,000 centimetres, or 250 metres.

A topographic map can show a track, a wooded area and contour lines near a village. Its key tells us what the symbols represent. A track symbol establishes that a mapped track exists; it does not automatically establish public permission, safe conditions or an open gate today. Use the information for the question it actually answers.

At 1:25,000, one centimetre represents 25,000 centimetres, or 250 metres. At 1:50,000 it represents 500 metres. At the same paper size, 1:25,000 usually offers more local detail over a smaller area. A larger denominator does not mean a larger-scale map.

Height and steepness differ

On screen: Height is a level above a reference. / Steepness compares rise with horizontal distance.

A summit can be high but reached by a gentle slope. A lower hill can have a steep side. Height describes a level, usually relative to a reference such as mean sea level. Steepness describes how quickly height changes over horizontal distance. Demonstrate two paths with the same rise but different horizontal lengths. The shorter horizontal path is steeper on average. Separating these ideas prevents us from calling the highest part of every profile the steepest simply because it is at the top.

Brief check: Is the highest point always on the steepest slope?
Listen for: No. Height and rate of height change are different.

Contours join equal heights

On screen: Each contour represents one height. / Read the contour interval.

A contour line joins points of equal height. The contour interval is the vertical difference between neighbouring contour levels. Find the interval before judging slope or counting levels. On a map with a fixed interval, closely spaced contours show a large height change across a short horizontal distance. Widely spaced ones show a gentler slope. Compare spacing within the same map first. Between different maps, interval and scale may differ, so spacing alone does not give a fair comparison of real steepness.

Brief check: What extra information matters when comparing different contour maps?
Listen for: Their contour intervals and horizontal scales.

A profile shows a side view

On screen: Horizontal axis: distance. / Vertical axis: height.

A profile turns height information along a chosen line into a side view. Mark the distance positions along the horizontal axis, then plot the corresponding heights on the vertical axis. Join the points to show the sampled shape. Both axes need labels and scales. The appearance of steepness can change if we exaggerate the vertical scale, so it is important to state how the drawing was made. A profile describes one selected line through the landscape; it does not show every direction across the whole hill.

Brief check: Which axis shows height?
Listen for: The vertical axis.

Compare rise over run

On screen: Rise = ending height − starting height. / Use the same horizontal distance for a direct comparison.

For equal horizontal intervals, the greatest rise identifies the steepest average interval. If the distances differ, compare both rise and run rather than the rise alone. A forty-metre rise over one hundred metres is steeper than the same rise over two hundred metres. Show the two right-angle triangles and describe the difference before calculating. Average slope summarises the interval and can hide smaller changes within it. Explain which section the conclusion refers to so pupils do not extend one result to the whole route.

Brief check: Which is steeper: the same rise over 100 m or 200 m?
Listen for: Over 100 m, because the height changes over a shorter horizontal distance.

A low hill can have a steep side

On screen: Compare two invented climbs. / On the same contour map, closely spaced contours show a greater height change over a shorter distance.

Compare two invented climbs. Hill A rises 200 metres over 2,000 horizontal metres. Hill B rises 80 metres over 200 horizontal metres. A is higher, but its rise per horizontal metre is 0.1; B’s is 0.4. B’s slope is steeper. Summit height tells us elevation, while gradient compares rise with horizontal distance.

On the same contour map, closely spaced contours show a greater height change over a shorter distance. Each contour joins equal heights, rather than showing a path to follow. A profile plots heights against distance to create a side view. Use matching axes to compare two profiles fairly.

Two angles locate a place

On screen: Does 20°N identify one unique place?

The Equator is the reference line for latitude. The prime meridian is the reference for longitude. A point at 20°N, 30°E lies north of the Equator and east of the prime meridian.

3–5 min · What this lesson explains

On screen: Follow the map, diagram and explanation. / No copying is needed. The printed sheet is optional. / The Equator is 0° latitude. / The prime meridian is 0° longitude. / Latitude first, longitude second.

Keep signs and directions consistent

On screen: Follow the map, diagram and explanation. / No copying is needed. The printed sheet is optional. / The Equator is 0° latitude. / The prime meridian is 0° longitude. / Latitude first, longitude second.

This lesson explains how to locate places using latitude and longitude. The worked example shows the method, and the scheduled case shows how it applies to a different situation. Read the three geographical ideas aloud, then connect each one to a feature in the visual. Students can follow the demonstration without producing a written answer.

5–8 min · Make the words clear

Words we will use

On screen: Latitude: Position north or south of the Equator / Longitude: Position east or west of the prime meridian / Equator: The line at zero degrees latitude

Latitude means position north or south of the equator. 20°N is north of the Equator.

Longitude means position east or west of the prime meridian. 30°W is west of the prime meridian.

Equator means the line at zero degrees latitude. 0° latitude separates north from south.

8–25 min · Teach the Geography

Latitude measures north or south

On screen: The Equator is 0° latitude. / Use N or S for non-zero latitude.

Latitude describes a position north or south of the Equator using an angle measured in degrees. The Equator is zero degrees latitude. Trace it around the globe, then point to a place north and a place south. Lines of latitude run around the globe, but the value tells us north-south position. This distinction can confuse learners: the direction of the line is not the direction represented by its value. Latitude alone does not identify one place because many places share the same latitude.

Brief check: Does 20°N identify one unique place?
Listen for: No. Many places share that latitude.

Longitude measures east or west

On screen: The prime meridian is 0° longitude. / Use E or W for non-zero longitude.

Longitude describes east-west position relative to the prime meridian. Meridians run between the poles, but the longitude value tells us how far east or west the location lies in angular terms. Point to the zero line, then compare a location east of it with one west of it. Do not confuse the letter E in longitude with a local journey direction: a point can have an eastern longitude and still travel west to another place. Coordinates describe locations within a global reference system.

Brief check: What does W mean in a longitude?
Listen for: West of the prime meridian.

Use both coordinates

On screen: Latitude first, longitude second. / Keep degrees and direction letters together.

A full coordinate pair joins north-south and east-west information. Twenty degrees north and thirty degrees east identifies the intersection of two reference lines. Build the answer in two parts and retain the direction letters. Twenty north, thirty west is a different place from twenty north, thirty east. At zero latitude the point is on the Equator; a north or south label is not needed to distinguish a hemisphere. Ask pupils to follow each line to the intersection rather than treating the pair as unrelated numbers.

Brief check: What changes if E is replaced by W?
Listen for: The point moves to the other side of the prime meridian at that longitude value.

Degrees are angles, not kilometres

On screen: Coordinate differences describe angular position. / Ground distance needs more information.

A difference of ten degrees is not automatically a fixed number of kilometres in every direction and location. In particular, meridians become closer towards the poles, so a degree of longitude represents different ground distances at different latitudes. Our introductory task locates places rather than calculating those distances. Emphasise the units: degrees for coordinates, metres or kilometres for ground length. Use this distinction to check an answer that labels a longitude difference in kilometres without a suitable calculation or location information.

Brief check: Can we simply replace degrees with kilometres?
Listen for: No. They are different quantities.

Two angles locate a place

On screen: The Equator is the reference line for latitude. / 20°N alone identifies many places around a latitude circle.

The Equator is the reference line for latitude. The prime meridian is the reference for longitude. A point at 20°N, 30°E lies north of the Equator and east of the prime meridian. Find the latitude line first, then the longitude line; their intersection locates the point.

20°N alone identifies many places around a latitude circle. Both coordinates and their directions are needed. Degrees measure angles, not a fixed number of kilometres. Meridians meet at the poles, so one degree of longitude spans a smaller ground distance at high latitudes than near the Equator.
