5–8 min · Make the words clear

Words we will use

On screen: Quality of life: How well people can live / Indicator: A measure used to compare conditions / Average: A summary that can hide differences

Quality of life means how well people can live. Consider services as well as income.

Indicator means a measure used to compare conditions. Travel time to a clinic is one indicator.

Average means a summary that can hide differences. The same mean can hide different incomes.

Words we will use

On screen: Capital: A city with a national government role / Function: An activity or role served by a place / Connection: A link between places or activities

Capital means a city with a national government role. A capital has a government role.

Function means an activity or role served by a place. A museum serves culture and learning.

Connection means a link between places or activities. Stations link homes to work and services.

Words we will use

On screen: Import: Goods entering a country / Export: Goods leaving a country / Trade: Buying and selling goods or services

Import means goods entering a country. Fruit arrives in the receiving country.

Export means goods leaving a country. The same fruit leaves the sending country.

Trade means buying and selling goods or services. Trace goods between seller and buyer.

8–25 min · Reconnect and explain

Quality of life has several dimensions

On screen: Health, safety, housing and access matter. / Income is one part of the picture.

Quality of life concerns how people live and experience their surroundings. Income matters, but health services, housing, safety, environmental conditions and access to opportunities also matter. A wealthy area may still have a long journey to a clinic or polluted surroundings. Introduce several indicators before judging a place. Explain that indicators measure selected aspects rather than a complete human experience. People can also value the same features differently, so factual measurements and personal priorities should be kept distinguishable.

Brief check: Does income alone tell us everything about quality of life?
Listen for: No. Other conditions and access also matter.

Averages can hide uneven experiences

On screen: An average describes a group. / It does not describe every person equally.

An average travel time can improve while some residents experience longer journeys. Use a central district and a remote district to illustrate this. If many people benefit, the overall average may fall even though a smaller group is worse off. A geographical evaluation should therefore examine the distribution of benefits and costs as well as the average. Ask who gains, who loses and where they live. This is especially important when deciding whether a new service location improves access fairly across an area.

Brief check: Can an improved average coexist with worse access for one district?
Listen for: Yes. Group averages can hide different local outcomes.

Explain the trade-off

On screen: A proposal can have benefits and costs. / Use evidence for both sides.

A new service may improve one condition while weakening another. For example, a larger central clinic could offer more facilities but increase travel for remote residents. Explain each effect through its mechanism rather than labelling the proposal simply good or bad. Then identify what evidence could help compare the effects: travel times, service capacity and the needs of different users. An opinion about priorities is legitimate, but it should be distinguished from a measurable claim about what the proposal will do.

Brief check: What should a balanced recommendation include?
Listen for: Supported benefits, supported costs and the needs of affected groups.

An average can hide a longer journey

On screen: Imagine four households whose clinic journeys are 10, 10, 10 and 50 minutes. / A new central clinic might offer more services while increasing travel for remote households.

Imagine four households whose clinic journeys are 10, 10, 10 and 50 minutes. The mean is 80 ÷ 4 = 20 minutes. Three households have much shorter journeys than the fourth. Reporting only the mean hides this uneven access. Quality of life includes access, health, housing, safety and environmental conditions as well as income.

A new central clinic might offer more services while increasing travel for remote households. Explain both effects. To judge the proposal, compare who benefits, who travels farther and which services change. A single average or income figure cannot describe every resident’s experience.

London is the UK’s capital

On screen: London is in south-east England, on the River Thames. / Its capital role includes national government.

London is the United Kingdom’s capital and lies in south-east England on the River Thames. Locate it within England, then within the UK, before discussing its functions. Parliament meets at Westminster, giving a concrete example of the city’s national government role. London is also a place where people live, work, study and visit. A capital is not defined as a place where everyone in the country lives or as the only city with important activities. Its role connects a particular location to national decision-making. Link the map location to the river and transport connections, while avoiding the assumption that river location alone completely explains the history or importance of the city.

Brief check: Does being the capital mean all UK residents live there?
Listen for: No. It describes the city’s national role.

A disruption can spread through the network

On screen: A closed link changes available routes. / Other services may face extra demand.

Close one bridge in a model town. Travellers may use another crossing, making it busier, or may be unable to reach their destination. Explain the chain from the original closure to the changed movement and possible effect on work or services. Do not assume every location is equally affected: some have alternative links and others do not. A good diagram traces the particular connections rather than saying that everything stops. Evidence about route use and alternatives helps identify the places most affected.

Brief check: Why might another bridge become busier after a closure?
Listen for: Some travellers divert to the remaining crossing.

Capacity must match demand over time

On screen: Capacity per trip is not capacity per hour. / Frequency tells us how often the service runs.

A bus carrying thirty passengers can move thirty per trip, but hourly capacity depends on how many trips it makes. If sixty people need to travel each hour, one trip may be insufficient while two full trips could match the stated demand. Real planning also considers timing, direction and accessibility. Distinguish the size of the vehicle from service frequency. This explains why drawing an alternative bus route does not establish that it can carry everyone displaced by a rail or bridge disruption.

Brief check: What must we know besides seats per bus?
Listen for: The frequency and timing of trips compared with demand.

What happens when a bridge closes?

On screen: A town links homes, workplaces, shops and services through a transport network. / An alternative bus with 30 seats running twice an hour offers at most 60 seats an hour in the stated direction.

A town links homes, workplaces, shops and services through a transport network. A bridge is one link. If it closes, some travellers divert to another crossing. The remaining route can become busier and journeys can lengthen. People with no suitable alternative may miss access to work or services. Trace the actual links rather than assuming the whole town stops.

An alternative bus with 30 seats running twice an hour offers at most 60 seats an hour in the stated direction. That is different from one 30-seat bus trip. Capacity, frequency and timing all matter. London illustrates a city with local functions alongside its national role as the UK capital.

The UK connects to the wider world

On screen: Imports enter; exports leave. / Travel and communication create other links.

An import enters a country from elsewhere; an export is sent to another country. Describe the direction from the country’s point of view. Fruit brought into a UK shop is an import for the UK, while the exporting place describes the same connection differently. Goods are only one kind of international link. People travel for visits, work, study or other purposes, and messages connect places without moving a person or parcel along the same physical route. Trace goods, people and information using separate arrows. The UK’s relationship with other countries therefore includes trade, tourism and communication rather than one single supply chain. Our invented examples illustrate those relationships without claiming a current national trade total or travel schedule.

Brief check: Can the same shipment be one country’s export and another’s import?
Listen for: Yes. The terms depend on the country’s point of view.

A broken link has immediate and later effects

On screen: First: the next stage lacks its input. / Later: other stages may be affected.

If a shipment of material is delayed, the first direct effect is on the stage waiting for that material. A factory may use stored stock temporarily, so production does not necessarily stop immediately. Later, fewer finished goods may reach shops. Trace the effects in order and state the conditions, such as how long stock lasts. Avoid claiming that every consumer is instantly affected by one delay. The network and its available reserves determine how the disruption spreads through time and across places.

Brief check: Why might the factory continue briefly after a delivery delay?
Listen for: It may have stored inputs available.

Alternatives involve trade-offs

On screen: Another route may keep goods moving. / It may add distance, time or cost.

A different port or supplier can restore a connection, but it may create new costs or delays. Compare the avoided disruption with the additional distance, price and environmental effects. Availability alone does not make the alternative best. A suitable recommendation identifies which link it repairs and what conditions still need checking. Distinguish classroom figures from real prices or service schedules. When a trade network changes, some places may gain business while others lose it, so a local benefit does not automatically describe every affected place.

Brief check: Does an available alternative necessarily have no disadvantages?
Listen for: No. It can add cost, time or other effects.

The geographical connection is this: A new central clinic might offer more services while increasing travel for remote households. Explain both effects. To judge the proposal, compare who benefits, who travels farther and which services change. A single average or income figure cannot describe every resident’s experience.

Change the example · 3.6

On screen: The access gap shrinks to 2 minutes. / Other differences and people’s needs remain.

Fictional neighbourhood A: average income 240 tokens, clinic 10 minutes away, no park. B: average income 255, clinic 35 minutes away, park nearby. These are averages and travel estimates, not descriptions of every resident.

The question is: New clinic cuts B’s journey to 12 minutes. What changes?

The access gap shrinks to 2 minutes. Other differences and people’s needs remain.

Teach the missing step · Case explained · 3.7

On screen: Correction: Alternative journey time and capacity. / The remaining connection may work with extra time or crowding; investigate its limits.

Here is the case we are explaining. Review case: A station closes but a bus route remains open. What should planners compare? Proposed answer: “Assume nobody can reach the area.”. Method note: A closed station removes one access point but not every city function. Trace an alternative route, count extra changes and identify who bears the cost. Visitors and commuters may experience different effects.

Correction: Alternative journey time and capacity. The remaining connection may work with extra time or crowding; investigate its limits. A complete response must explain the method, not simply copy the correct choice. For a changed case, accept different answers only when the new condition actually supports them.

The geographical connection is this: An alternative bus with 30 seats running twice an hour offers at most 60 seats an hour in the stated direction. That is different from one 30-seat bus trip. Capacity, frequency and timing all matter. London illustrates a city with local functions alongside its national role as the UK capital.

Change the example · 3.7

On screen: Often other links exist, but the source does not confirm their availability. / Investigate alternatives.

Fictional city network: homes connect to a station, museum, council office and market. Today the museum is closed. A group needs a class visit. No alternative timetable or access report has been supplied.

The question is: Can a city still function when one facility closes?

Often other links exist, but the source does not confirm their availability. Investigate alternatives.

Teach the missing step · Case explained · 3.8

On screen: Correction: Imports. / The goods enter the UK; the same movement is an export for the sending country.

Here is the case we are explaining. Review case: A UK shop receives goods from another country. From the UK viewpoint, these are what? Proposed answer: “Exports.”. Method note: A shipment leaving A and entering B is an export for A and an import for B. A message may travel without the goods moving yet. Label the arrow type and whose viewpoint defines the trade word.

Correction: Imports. The goods enter the UK; the same movement is an export for the sending country. A complete response must explain the method, not simply copy the correct choice. For a changed case, accept different answers only when the new condition actually supports them.

The geographical connection is this: If fabric is delayed, the garment maker is the next stage directly affected. Stored fabric may keep production going for a while. Later effects depend on the delay and reserves. Another supplier or route could help, but may change cost, time or environmental effects. The shop’s location is not necessarily the product’s origin.

Change the example · 3.8

On screen: No. / Different flows can use different networks.

Fictional trade: apples move from Country A to Country B. Payment moves back. An order message travels online. A worker separately travels to visit relatives. A port then closes.

The question is: Does a port closure automatically stop online messages?

No. Different flows can use different networks.

36–39 min · Brief spoken checks

What should a balanced recommendation include?

On screen: Think about the explanation. Answer aloud when invited.

A new service may improve one condition while weakening another. For example, a larger central clinic could offer more facilities but increase travel for remote residents. Explain each effect through its mechanism rather than labelling the proposal simply good or bad. Then identify what evidence could help compare the effects: travel times, service capacity and the needs of different users. An opinion about priorities is legitimate, but it should be distinguished from a measurable claim about what the proposal will do.

Listen for this distinction: Supported benefits, supported costs and the needs of affected groups.

What must we know besides seats per bus?

On screen: Think about the explanation. Answer aloud when invited.

A bus carrying thirty passengers can move thirty per trip, but hourly capacity depends on how many trips it makes. If sixty people need to travel each hour, one trip may be insufficient while two full trips could match the stated demand. Real planning also considers timing, direction and accessibility. Distinguish the size of the vehicle from service frequency. This explains why drawing an alternative bus route does not establish that it can carry everyone displaced by a rail or bridge disruption.

Listen for this distinction: The frequency and timing of trips compared with demand.

Does an available alternative necessarily have no disadvantages?

On screen: Think about the explanation. Answer aloud when invited.

A different port or supplier can restore a connection, but it may create new costs or delays. Compare the avoided disruption with the additional distance, price and environmental effects. Availability alone does not make the alternative best. A suitable recommendation identifies which link it repairs and what conditions still need checking. Distinguish classroom figures from real prices or service schedules. When a trade network changes, some places may gain business while others lose it, so a local benefit does not automatically describe every affected place.

Listen for this distinction: No. It can add cost, time or other effects.

Landscape evidence file

7B · Week 18 · Lesson 1 · sections 4.1

40-minute planning estimate: introduction 3, goal 2, vocabulary 3, explanation 17, worked examples 7, case explanation 4, spoken checks 3, recap 1. Divide each block between topics in combined lessons. Adjust to the class; elapsed classroom teaching time has not been measured.

0–3 min · Introduce the geographical question

A valley can preserve an older story

On screen: Was the ice extent identical everywhere throughout Britain’s history?

A broad valley with steep sides, a hanging tributary valley and transported boulders can provide clues about former ice. A glacier can widen and deepen a pre-existing valley while carrying rock debris. When the ice disappears, the altered landforms remain.

3–5 min · What this lesson explains

Build a past-ice explanation from several clues

On screen: Follow the map, diagram and explanation. / No copying is needed. The printed sheet is optional. / Past cold periods brought extensive ice to parts of Britain. / Moving ice can erode and transport material. / Valley shape is one clue.

This lesson explains how to use evidence to investigate past glaciation. The worked example shows the method, and the scheduled case shows how it applies to a different situation. Read the three geographical ideas aloud, then connect each one to a feature in the visual. Students can follow the demonstration without producing a written answer.

5–8 min · Make the words clear

Words we will use

On screen: Glaciation: A period when ice covers an area / Ice sheet: A large mass of ice covering land / Evidence: Information supporting an explanation

Glaciation means a period when ice covers an area. Ice can shape land and later retreat.

Ice sheet means a large mass of ice covering land. Ice covers a broad area of land.

Evidence means information supporting an explanation. Scratches and deposits support an ice explanation.

8–25 min · Teach the Geography

Britain has a glacial history

On screen: Past cold periods brought extensive ice to parts of Britain. / The present landscape contains evidence of those changes.

Britain experienced repeated periods of glaciation during the Quaternary, with extensive ice affecting much of northern and central Britain at different times. The school-plan question about twenty thousand years ago introduces a landscape very different from today’s. Do not treat Britain as entirely covered by an identical glacier at every stage: extent and timing varied. The important introductory connection is between colder past conditions, moving ice and surviving landforms or deposits. Many valleys now occupied by rivers were modified by earlier ice. To reconstruct a particular place at a particular date, we need dated and mapped geological evidence rather than only a modern photograph. This gives the past-ice investigation a regional context before pupils examine individual clues.

Brief check: Was the ice extent identical everywhere throughout Britain’s history?
Listen for: No. Extent and timing varied.

Ice can change a landscape

On screen: Moving ice can erode and transport material. / Landforms can remain after the ice melts.

A glacier is moving land ice, and it can change the ground beneath and around it. Its erosion can alter valley shapes, while transported material can be deposited as the ice melts. The ice does not have to remain for all traces of its activity to disappear. Introduce the difference between an active process and a landform left behind. A modern valley photograph may contain clues to past ice, but identifying that history requires more than assuming every mountain valley was made entirely by glaciers.

Brief check: Can a landform remain after the glacier disappears?
Listen for: Yes. The resulting shape or deposits can remain.

Use several clues for past ice

On screen: Valley shape is one clue. / Deposits and mapped evidence add information.

A broad valley with steep sides may be consistent with glacial erosion, but one view does not provide a complete history. Deposits, rock surfaces, surrounding landforms and geological mapping can add independent evidence. Explain how several compatible clues support a claim more strongly than a single vague resemblance. A deposit also needs interpretation: not all sediment in a glaciated area was dropped directly by ice. We should identify what each source shows and which part of the historical explanation it supports.

Brief check: Why use more than one clue?
Listen for: Different evidence can test and strengthen the proposed explanation.

Separate appearance from history

On screen: “The valley has steep sides” is an observation. / “Ice eroded it” is a historical explanation.

Point to the visible shape and describe it before offering a cause. The photograph can show a broad floor and steep sides, but it cannot directly show an event that happened before the photograph was taken. Historical explanation connects the appearance to processes using further evidence. Keep the two sentence types distinct so pupils understand why an accurate description is valuable without being complete proof of a cause. A confident explanation should be proportional to the sources available, not to how familiar the picture seems.

Brief check: Can a photograph directly show when a valley was eroded?
Listen for: Not by its shape alone.

Time and change need evidence

On screen: Ask when ice was present. / Ask what changed before and after it.

To reconstruct a landscape’s history, arrange evidence in time as well as space. A dated deposit can help establish when material was laid down. Earlier and later sources can show changes in ice extent or valley conditions. Explain that a landform may reflect several processes acting at different times. A river can occupy a valley previously modified by ice. The present process and the earlier process therefore need not be competing explanations of exactly the same stage. Specify the part of the history being claimed.

Brief check: Can a river now flow through a valley previously modified by ice?
Listen for: Yes. Processes can act at different times.

A valley can preserve an older story

On screen: A broad valley with steep sides, a hanging tributary valley and transported boulders can provide clues about former ice. / One U-shaped outline is not a complete historical investigation.

A broad valley with steep sides, a hanging tributary valley and transported boulders can provide clues about former ice. A glacier can widen and deepen a pre-existing valley while carrying rock debris. When the ice disappears, the altered landforms remain. Parts of Britain therefore have glacial landscapes even where no glacier exists today.

One U-shaped outline is not a complete historical investigation. Compare several landforms, deposits, rock evidence and reliable regional research. Separate what is visible now from the process inferred to have formed it. A photograph records appearance; dates and history require further evidence.

One U-shaped outline is not a complete historical investigation. Compare several landforms, deposits, rock evidence and reliable regional research. Separate what is visible now from the process inferred to have formed it. A photograph records appearance; dates and history require further evidence.

A photograph records appearance; dates and history require further evidence.

Keep the glacier in balance

7B · Week 19 · Lesson 1 · sections 4.2

40-minute planning estimate: introduction 3, goal 2, vocabulary 3, explanation 17, worked examples 7, case explanation 4, spoken checks 3, recap 1. Divide each block between topics in combined lessons. Adjust to the class; elapsed classroom teaching time has not been measured.

0–3 min · Introduce the geographical question

A retreating glacier still moves

On screen: Why can glaciers exist in some high mountains outside polar regions?

Snow that survives summer can accumulate, become compressed and gradually form glacier ice. Gravity drives ice flow downhill. Accumulation adds mass; ablation removes it through processes including melting and sublimation.

3–5 min · What this lesson explains

Calculate glacier mass balance

On screen: Follow the map, diagram and explanation. / No copying is needed. The printed sheet is optional. / They need conditions in which snow and ice can remain. / Snow accumulates and is compressed. / Accumulation adds snow or ice.

This lesson explains how to explain glacier movement and calculate ice balance. The worked example shows the method, and the scheduled case shows how it applies to a different situation. Read the three geographical ideas aloud, then connect each one to a feature in the visual. Students can follow the demonstration without producing a written answer.

5–8 min · Make the words clear

Words we will use

On screen: Glacier: A mass of land ice that moves / Accumulation: Snow and ice added to a glacier / Ablation: Snow and ice lost through melting and other processes

Glacier means a mass of land ice that moves. Ice flows downhill under gravity.

Accumulation means snow and ice added to a glacier. Snow adds to the ice store.

Ablation means snow and ice lost through melting and other processes. Melting removes ice from the store.

8–25 min · Teach the Geography

Where can glaciers persist?

On screen: They need conditions in which snow and ice can remain. / They occur in polar regions and some high mountains.

Glaciers occur where conditions allow enough snow and ice to persist and accumulate. Polar regions provide examples, as do high mountain areas in several parts of the world. A high mountain near the Equator can have colder conditions than nearby low land, so latitude alone is insufficient to explain every glacier location. Temperature, elevation and snowfall all matter. A cold dry place may receive little snow, while a place with large snowfall may support ice under a different balance of conditions. Start by locating polar regions and mountain examples on the world view, then explain the accumulation and loss relationship. The existence of ice does not make every frozen lake a glacier: glacier ice also moves under its own weight.

Brief check: Why can glaciers exist in some high mountains outside polar regions?
Listen for: High elevation can provide cold conditions, alongside sufficient snow accumulation.

Snow can become glacier ice

On screen: Snow accumulates and is compressed. / A glacier moves under its own weight.

Where snow persists and accumulates, it can become compacted into denser ice over time. A glacier forms and moves under its own weight. It is not simply any patch of snow that lasts for a few days. Explain the distinction between stored ice and its movement. Ice can flow slowly even when the glacier’s front appears nearly stationary. The front, called the snout or terminus, is a boundary whose position depends on both ice arriving and ice being lost near it.

Brief check: Is a stationary-looking front proof that no ice moves?
Listen for: No. Flow and front position are different.

Accumulation and ablation

On screen: Accumulation adds snow or ice. / Ablation removes glacier mass.

Accumulation adds mass, commonly through snowfall. Ablation removes mass through processes such as melting, sublimation or ice breaking away in relevant settings. In the classroom model we simplify these processes to additions and losses. Make that simplification explicit before using tokens or blocks. The glacier can gain or lose stored mass depending on the balance over a stated period. Its actual response also depends on where the changes happen and how ice flows, so a simple total is useful without representing every physical detail.

Brief check: What does accumulation do to glacier mass?
Listen for: It adds mass.

Calculate a simplified balance

On screen: Balance = additions − losses. / A negative result means net loss in this model.

Suppose the model gains nine units and loses six over the same period. Nine minus six is three units of net gain. Reverse the values and the balance becomes negative three. State the units and period, then explain the sign rather than asking pupils only to perform subtraction. A zero balance means the stated additions and losses are equal, not that all processes stop. Ice can continue entering and leaving while the total remains unchanged. This connects a calculation to the process it represents.

Brief check: Does a zero balance mean no ice is added or lost?
Listen for: No. Equal additions and losses can occur.

Movement and retreat can coexist

On screen: Ice can flow forwards. / The snout can retreat when loss exceeds supply there.

At the front, compare the arrival of ice with the rate at which it is removed. If more is lost than supplied, the boundary can move backwards even while ice flows towards it. A retreating glacier still moves

On screen: Why can glaciers exist in some high mountains outside polar regions?

3–5 min · What this lesson explains

Separate ice movement from the snout's position

On screen: Follow the map, diagram and explanation. / No copying is needed. The printed sheet is optional. / They need conditions in which snow and ice can remain. / Snow accumulates and is compressed. / Accumulation adds snow or ice.

This lesson explains how to explain glacier movement and calculate ice balance. The worked example shows the method, and the scheduled case shows how it applies to a different situation. Read the three geographical ideas aloud, then connect each one to a feature in the visual. Students can follow the demonstration without producing a written answer.

5–8 min · Make the words clear

Words we will use

On screen: Glacier: A mass of land ice that moves / Accumulation: Snow and ice added to a glacier / Ablation: Snow and ice lost through melting and other processes

Glacier means a mass of land ice that moves. Ice flows downhill under gravity.

Accumulation means snow and ice added to a glacier. Snow adds to the ice store.

Ablation means snow and ice lost through melting and other processes. Melting removes ice from the store.

8–25 min · Teach the Geography

Where can glaciers persist?

On screen: They need conditions in which snow and ice can remain. / They occur in polar regions and some high mountains.

Glaciers occur where conditions allow enough snow and ice to persist and accumulate. Polar regions provide examples, as do high mountain areas in several parts of the world. A high mountain near the Equator can have colder conditions than nearby low land, so latitude alone is insufficient to explain every glacier location. Temperature, elevation and snowfall all matter. A cold dry place may receive little snow, while a place with large snowfall may support ice under a different balance of conditions. Start by locating polar regions and mountain examples on the world view, then explain the accumulation and loss relationship. The existence of ice does not make every frozen lake a glacier: glacier ice also moves under its own weight.

Brief check: Why can glaciers exist in some high mountains outside polar regions?
Listen for: High elevation can provide cold conditions, alongside sufficient snow accumulation.

Snow can become glacier ice

On screen: Snow accumulates and is compressed. / A glacier moves under its own weight.

Where snow persists and accumulates, it can become compacted into denser ice over time. A glacier forms and moves under its own weight. It is not simply any patch of snow that lasts for a few days. Explain the distinction between stored ice and its movement. Ice can flow slowly even when the glacier’s front appears nearly stationary. The front, called the snout or terminus, is a boundary whose position depends on both ice arriving and ice being lost near it.

Brief check: Is a stationary-looking front proof that no ice moves?
Listen for: No. Flow and front position are different.

Accumulation and ablation

On screen: Accumulation adds snow or ice. / Ablation removes glacier mass.

Accumulation adds mass, commonly through snowfall. Ablation removes mass through processes such as melting, sublimation or ice breaking away in relevant settings. In the classroom model we simplify these processes to additions and losses. Make that simplification explicit before using tokens or blocks. The glacier can gain or lose stored mass depending on the balance over a stated period. Its actual response also depends on where the changes happen and how ice flows, so a simple total is useful without representing every physical detail.

Brief check: What does accumulation do to glacier mass?
Listen for: It adds mass.

Calculate a simplified balance

On screen: Balance = additions − losses. / A negative result means net loss in this model.

Suppose the model gains nine units and loses six over the same period. Nine minus six is three units of net gain. Reverse the values and the balance becomes negative three. State the units and period, then explain the sign rather than asking pupils only to perform subtraction. A zero balance means the stated additions and losses are equal, not that all processes stop. Ice can continue entering and leaving while the total remains unchanged. This connects a calculation to the process it represents.

Brief check: Does a zero balance mean no ice is added or lost?
Listen for: No. Equal additions and losses can occur.

Movement and retreat can coexist

On screen: Ice can flow forwards. / The snout can retreat when loss exceeds supply there.

At the front, compare the arrival of ice with the rate at which it is removed. If more is lost than supplied, the boundary can move backwards even while ice flows towards it. Use a moving conveyor with an end being removed as an analogy, then identify its limits: real glaciers involve complex flow and changing geometry. Avoid saying that glacier retreat is ice flowing uphill. Retreat describes the boundary’s position, while flow describes the motion of the ice itself. A simple annual balance does not predict an exact retreat distance.

Brief check: Can a glacier retreat while ice still flows towards its front?
Listen for: Yes. Loss at the front can exceed incoming supply.

A retreating glacier still moves

On screen: Snow that survives summer can accumulate, become compressed and gradually form glacier ice. / The snout can retreat uphill while the ice itself continues flowing downhill, because loss at the front exceeds the arrival of ice.

Snow that survives summer can accumulate, become compressed and gradually form glacier ice. Gravity drives ice flow downhill. Accumulation adds mass; ablation removes it through processes including melting and sublimation. In an invented budget, 12 units enter and 15 leave: the store loses 3 units.

The snout can retreat uphill while the ice itself continues flowing downhill, because loss at the front exceeds the arrival of ice. Retreat describes the changing position of the glacier’s end, not reversed ice flow. Short-term snowfall and longer-term mass balance both affect the system.

Retreat describes the changing edge position, not the direction of every particle.

The snout can retreat uphill while the ice itself continues flowing downhill, because loss at the front exceeds the arrival of ice. Retreat describes the changing position of the glacier’s end, not reversed ice flow. Short-term snowfall and longer-term mass balance both affect the system.

Retreat describes the changing edge position, not the direction of every particle.

The difference matters because the snout can retreat uphill while the ice itself continues flowing downhill, because loss at the front exceeds the arrival of ice. 7B · Week 20 · Lesson 1 · sections 4.3

40-minute planning estimate: introduction 3, goal 2, vocabulary 3, explanation 17, worked examples 7, case explanation 4, spoken checks 3, recap 1. Divide each block between topics in combined lessons. Adjust to the class; elapsed classroom teaching time has not been measured.

0–3 min · Introduce the geographical question

Two ways moving ice wears rock

On screen: Which term involves removing material?

A glacier can freeze onto loosened rock and pull fragments away as it moves: plucking. Rock fragments carried at the glacier base can scrape bedrock: abrasion. The ice supplies movement while debris acts as the abrasive tool.

3–5 min · What this lesson explains

Distinguish plucking, transport and abrasion

On screen: Follow the map, diagram and explanation. / No copying is needed. The printed sheet is optional. / Weathering breaks rock down in place. / Ice can grip loosened rock. / Rock carried by ice can scrape the bed.

This lesson explains how to explain glacial erosion as a sequence of actions. The worked example shows the method, and the scheduled case shows how it applies to a different situation. Read the three geographical ideas aloud, then connect each one to a feature in the visual. Students can follow the demonstration without producing a written answer.

5–8 min · Make the words clear

Words we will use

On screen: Plucking: Ice pulling loosened rock away / Abrasion: Rock carried by ice scraping the ground / Erosion: Wearing away and removing material

Plucking means ice pulling loosened rock away. Ice removes a loosened rock block.

Abrasion means rock carried by ice scraping the ground. Debris scrapes grooves into bedrock.

Erosion means wearing away and removing material. Removal and wear change the rock surface.

8–25 min · Teach the Geography

Erosion differs from weathering

On screen: Weathering breaks rock down in place. / Erosion removes and transports material.

Weathering breaks rock down where it lies. Erosion includes removal by an agent such as moving ice or water. A glacier can pick up material already loosened by weathering and move it to another location. Distinguish the terms using one rock at the valley side: breaking it into pieces is not the same as carrying those pieces away. In an actual landscape, the processes can interact. Keeping their roles clear helps pupils build an explanation of change rather than treating every kind of rock damage as one identical action.

Brief check: Which term involves removing material?
Listen for: Erosion.

Plucking removes rock fragments

On screen: Ice can grip loosened rock. / Movement can pull fragments away.

Plucking is the removal of rock fragments by moving glacier ice. Water can enter cracks and freezing conditions can help loosen rock, while ice can become attached to parts of the bed. As the glacier moves, fragments may be pulled away. Use the diagram to show the original crack, the removed fragment and its new position. This is a simplified account: conditions beneath a glacier vary. The key distinction is removal of pieces rather than merely scratching the surface. Those pieces can then become tools for further erosion.

Brief check: What does plucking remove?
Listen for: Fragments of rock from the bed or sides.

Abrasion wears the surface

On screen: Rock carried by ice can scrape the bed. / Friction can scratch and smooth rock.

Abrasion occurs when debris carried by the glacier rubs or scrapes the ground. Compare it with sandpaper wearing a surface: the particles do the scraping as the moving material presses them against the rock. Glacial scratches can provide evidence of past motion, but their interpretation requires an appropriate source and context. Explain how plucking can supply fragments that later contribute to abrasion. The two processes are connected without being the same action. A classroom scraper illustrates friction but does not reproduce the full glacier system.

Brief check: How does abrasion differ from plucking?
Listen for: Abrasion wears or scratches surfaces; plucking removes fragments.

A model must control the comparison

On screen: Change one factor at a time. / Keep force and material comparable.

If we compare a rough and smooth scraper but push the rough one much harder, we cannot isolate roughness as the explanation for different wear. Force changed too. Explain a fair comparison using the same surface, movement and force while changing the feature being tested. The model then supports a limited statement about that setup. It cannot establish the exact erosion rate of a real glacier. Useful models clarify a mechanism, and their limitations tell us which extra processes and conditions are missing.

Brief check: Can roughness alone explain a result if force also changed?
Listen for: No. The comparison changed more than one factor.

Two ways moving ice wears rock

On screen: A glacier can freeze onto loosened rock and pull fragments away as it moves: plucking. / Weathering breaks or weakens rock in place.

A glacier can freeze onto loosened rock and pull fragments away as it moves: plucking. Rock fragments carried at the glacier base can scrape bedrock: abrasion. The ice supplies movement while debris acts as the abrasive tool. These processes remove or wear material; they are forms of erosion.

Weathering breaks or weakens rock in place. Erosion involves removal. In a classroom scraping model, keep load, surface and number of strokes consistent when comparing materials. A model can illustrate an action without reproducing the full pressure, time scale or behaviour of a real glacier.

25–32 min · Work through the examples

Worked example · 4.3

On screen: Plucking removes blocks loosened from bedrock; transport carries debris; abrasion occurs when debris held by moving ice scrapes the bed. / Label each action separately so “erosion” does not hide the mechanism.

Plucking removes blocks loosened from bedrock; transport carries debris; abrasion occurs when debris held by moving ice scrapes the bed. Label each action separately so “erosion” does not hide the mechanism.

Moving debris can wear and scratch rock surfaces.

Weathering breaks or weakens rock in place. Erosion involves removal. In a classroom scraping model, keep load, surface and number of strokes consistent when comparing materials. A model can illustrate an action without reproducing the full pressure, time scale or behaviour of a real glacier.

Explain the contrast

On screen: Which action best represents abrasion?

Response A: Rock fragments carried in ice scrape bedrock.

Moving debris can wear and scratch rock surfaces.

Compare it with response B: A glacier simply holds still without contact.. The difference matters because weathering breaks or weakens rock in place. Erosion involves removal. In a classroom scraping model, keep load, surface and number of strokes consistent when comparing materials. A model can illustrate an action without reproducing the full pressure, time scale or behaviour of a real glacier.

Weathering breaks or weakens rock in place. Erosion involves removal. In a classroom scraping model, keep load, surface and number of strokes consistent when comparing materials. A model can illustrate an action without reproducing the full pressure, time scale or behaviour of a real glacier.

32–36 min · Explain the scheduled case

Case explained · 4.3

On screen: Removal is plucking; carriage is transport; scraping by debris is abrasion.

Here is the case we are explaining. A loosened block freezes into ice, moves downhill and scratches bedrock.

Removal is plucking; carriage is transport; scraping by debris is abrasion.

The geographical connection is this: Weathering breaks or weakens rock in place. Erosion involves removal. In a classroom scraping model, keep load, surface and number of strokes consistent when comparing materials. A model can illustrate an action without reproducing the full pressure, time scale or behaviour of a real glacier.

On screen: Deposition: the carried material is left behind.

A fictional glacier slides over cracked rock. One block freezes into the ice and is removed; carried debris scratches other surfaces.

The question is: What happens when ice melts and releases the debris?

Deposition: the carried material is left behind.

Explain a fair comparison using the same surface, movement and force while changing the feature being tested. The model then supports a limited statement about that setup. It cannot establish the exact erosion rate of a real glacier. Useful models clarify a mechanism, and their limitations tell us which extra processes and conditions are missing.

Listen for this distinction: No. The comparison changed more than one factor.

On screen: Give a short explanation when invited.

Rock fragments carried in ice scrape bedrock.

Moving debris can wear and scratch rock surfaces.

Plucking removes blocks loosened from bedrock; transport carries debris; abrasion occurs when debris held by moving ice scrapes the bed. Label each action separately so “erosion” does not hide the mechanism.

What this case teaches

On screen: Follow the teacher’s demonstration on the map.

A glacier can freeze onto loosened rock and pull fragments away as it moves: plucking. Rock fragments carried at the glacier base can scrape bedrock: abrasion. The ice supplies movement while debris acts as the abrasive tool. These processes remove or wear material; they are forms of erosion.

Weathering breaks or weakens rock in place. Erosion involves removal. In a classroom scraping model, keep load, surface and number of strokes consistent when comparing materials. A model can illustrate an action without reproducing the full pressure, time scale or behaviour of a real glacier.

32–36 min · Explain the scheduled case

Case explained · 4.3

On screen: B has abrasive material. / Real erosion also depends on speed, pressure, temperature and rock conditions.

Here is the case we are explaining. Model A contains no rock fragments; B carries angular debris against the bed.

B has abrasive material. Real erosion also depends on speed, pressure, temperature and rock conditions.

The geographical connection is this: Weathering breaks or weakens rock in place. Erosion involves removal. In a classroom scraping model, keep load, surface and number of strokes consistent when comparing materials. A model can illustrate an action without reproducing the full pressure, time scale or behaviour of a real glacier.

Change the example · 4.3

On screen: Deposition: the carried material is left behind.

A fictional glacier carries sharp rock fragments at its base. The fragments scrape the bed. Elsewhere, ice removes a loosened block.

The question is: What happens when ice melts and releases the debris?

Deposition: the carried material is left behind.

36–39 min · Brief spoken checks

Can roughness alone explain a result if force also changed?

On screen: Think about the explanation. Answer aloud when invited.

If we compare a rough and smooth scraper but push the rough one much harder, we cannot isolate roughness as the explanation for different wear. Force changed too. Explain a fair comparison using the same surface, movement and force while changing the feature being tested. The model then supports a limited statement about that setup. It cannot establish the exact erosion rate of a real glacier. Useful models clarify a mechanism, and their limitations tell us which extra processes and conditions are missing.

Listen for this distinction: No. The comparison changed more than one factor.

Which comparison isolates the effect of debris in a classroom scraping model?

On screen: Give a short explanation when invited.

Same force and distance, different surface roughness.

Holding other conditions constant makes the effect of the changed factor easier to interpret.

Sandpaper sliding over a surface models scraping better than a smooth block, but real erosion also depends on pressure, speed, rock and debris. Change one model factor at a time to make a fair comparison.

No. The comparison changed more than one factor.

Change the valley shape

7B · Week 21 · Lesson 1 · sections 4.4

40-minute planning estimate: introduction 3, goal 2, vocabulary 3, explanation 17, worked examples 7, case explanation 4, spoken checks 3, recap 1. Divide each block between topics in combined lessons. Adjust to the class; elapsed classroom teaching time has not been measured.

0–3 min · Introduce the geographical question

Why the tributary valley hangs

On screen: Why can the tributary valley floor lie above the main floor?

A main glacier and a smaller tributary glacier meet. The larger glacier can erode the main valley more deeply, leaving the tributary floor at a higher level. After the ice melts, a stream from the tributary may fall into the main valley as a waterfall.

3–5 min · What this lesson explains

Explain widening and deepening in cross-section

On screen: Follow the map, diagram and explanation. / No copying is needed. The printed sheet is optional. / A tributary valley can meet a deeper main trough. / Ridges can project into an earlier valley. / Compare the floor and both sides.

This lesson explains how to explain glacial valley shapes using the correct viewpoint. The worked example shows the method, and the scheduled case shows how it applies to a different situation. Read the three geographical ideas aloud, then connect each one to a feature in the visual. Students can follow the demonstration without producing a written answer.

5–8 min · Make the words clear

Words we will use

On screen: U-shaped valley: A broad, steep-sided valley shaped by ice / Hanging valley: A tributary valley above the main valley floor / Truncated spur: A ridge end cut short by moving ice

U-shaped valley means a broad, steep-sided valley shaped by ice. Compare a broad floor and steep sides.

Hanging valley means a tributary valley above the main valley floor. A tributary joins above the main valley floor.

Truncated spur means a ridge end cut short by moving ice. Ice cuts across the end of a ridge.

8–25 min · Teach the Geography

Hanging valleys show different erosion levels

On screen: A tributary valley can meet a deeper main trough. / Its floor may remain above the main valley floor.

A smaller tributary glacier may erode less deeply than a larger glacier in the main valley. After the ice disappears, the tributary valley floor can lie above the deeper main trough. This is called a hanging valley. Trace the two floors and their height difference. A stream may drop from the higher tributary towards the lower main floor, sometimes creating a waterfall. The explanation concerns different amounts of erosion in connected valleys; it is not a valley floating without support. Use the cross-section or a suitable diagram to show the relationship clearly before introducing the name. The landform joins local shapes to the wider glacier system that once occupied the valleys.

Brief check: Why can the tributary valley floor lie above the main floor?
Listen for: The main glacier may have eroded its valley more deeply.

Truncated spurs mark altered valley sides

On screen: Ridges can project into an earlier valley. / Glacial erosion can cut back their ends.

A spur is a ridge projecting from a valley side. A river valley may wind around interlocking spurs, while a large glacier moving through the valley can erode their projecting ends. The cut-back faces are called truncated spurs. Show a plan view with projecting ridges before the altered trough. Explain why this landform needs a different view from a simple profile across the floor. It helps pupils connect three-dimensional landscape features rather than treating every glacial feature as the same letter-shaped cross-section. In a real landscape, suitable evidence is needed to identify the shape and its history; the schematic clarifies the proposed mechanism.

Brief check: What part of the spur is described as truncated?
Listen for: Its projecting end has been cut back.

A valley cross-section looks across

On screen: Compare the floor and both sides. / The viewing direction matters.

A cross-section shows the shape across a valley rather than along its length. Mark one side, the floor and the other side. A photograph looking down the valley may not reveal that profile clearly, so source choice matters. A river and glacier can both occupy a valley without producing the same typical cross-section. Begin with description: is the floor narrow or broad, and how do the sides rise? Then connect the form to the processes that may have modified it, using suitable evidence.

Brief check: Which view best tests a cross-section claim?
Listen for: A view or profile across the valley.

River valleys are often V-shaped

On screen: River erosion cuts into the valley floor. / Slope processes affect the sides.

Many upper river valleys have narrow floors and sloping sides, giving a V-shaped cross-section. Downward river erosion and material moving from the sides both contribute to the form. Explain that the letter is a simplified description, not an exact geometry found everywhere. Other factors such as rock, structure and past processes affect actual valleys. Point to the narrow channel and the slopes so pupils understand what the label describes. A V shape is a useful pattern for comparison rather than proof that one agent explains the entire history.

Brief check: What part of a typical V-shaped profile is narrow?
Listen for: The valley floor.

Glaciers widen and deepen valleys

On screen: Ice occupies much of the valley. / Erosion can make a broad trough.

A valley glacier can occupy a large part of a valley rather than being confined to a narrow water channel. Erosion at the bed and sides can deepen and widen the valley, producing a glacial trough with a broad floor and steep sides. The common U-shaped label summarises that cross-section. Trace the contact areas before showing the changed profile. Do not say ice merely sits in the valley and leaves the shape unchanged. The form results from interaction between moving ice, carried debris and the rock it encounters.

Brief check: Why can ice affect more of the valley profile than a narrow channel?
Listen for: A glacier can occupy and erode a much broader part of the valley.

Describe the form before claiming the cause

On screen: Broad floor and steep sides describe shape. / Further evidence supports the glacial history.

A pupil can correctly describe a broad floor without yet proving its origin. Link the description to a process explanation, then identify evidence that would support past glacier activity. Compare a suitable cross-profile with a view along the floor and explain why one source answers the shape question more directly. Real valleys can have complex histories and later river changes. A useful answer states the form observed, the proposed process and the evidence available, instead of using the word glacier as a substitute for explanation.

Brief check: Does every broad valley photograph prove a complete glacial history?
Listen for: No. Use appropriate additional evidence.

Why the tributary valley hangs

On screen: A main glacier and a smaller tributary glacier meet. / A U-shaped cross-section is a slice across the valley: steep sides and a relatively broad floor.

A main glacier and a smaller tributary glacier meet. The larger glacier can erode the main valley more deeply, leaving the tributary floor at a higher level. After the ice melts, a stream from the tributary may fall into the main valley as a waterfall. The difference in valley-floor height explains the hanging valley.

A U-shaped cross-section is a slice across the valley: steep sides and a relatively broad floor. It is not a river bend viewed from above. Glacial erosion can also cut back interlocking spurs, leaving truncated ends along the main valley sides.

Carve a mountain

7B · Week 22 · Lesson 1 · sections 4.5

40-minute planning estimate: introduction 3, goal 2, vocabulary 3, explanation 17, worked examples 7, case explanation 4, spoken checks 3, recap 1. Divide each block between topics in combined lessons. Adjust to the class; elapsed classroom teaching time has not been measured.

0–3 min · Introduce the geographical question

Build the landforms from the hollow out

On screen: Is the corrie the ridge or the hollow?

Snow collects in a mountain hollow. As ice develops and moves, erosion deepens the hollow and steepens its back wall, forming a corrie. After melting, water may occupy the hollow as a tarn.

3–5 min · What this lesson explains

Explain a corrie and the ridge between hollows

On screen: Follow the map, diagram and explanation. / No copying is needed. The printed sheet is optional. / A corrie is a bowl-like hollow. / Erosion acts on neighbouring hollows. / Erosion can act on several sides.

This lesson explains how to describe and explain glacial mountain features. The worked example shows the method, and the scheduled case shows how it applies to a different situation. Read the three geographical ideas aloud, then connect each one to a feature in the visual. Students can follow the demonstration without producing a written answer.

5–8 min · Make the words clear

Words we will use

On screen: Corrie: An armchair-shaped hollow carved by ice / Arête: A sharp ridge between glacial hollows / Pyramidal peak: A pointed peak eroded from several sides

Corrie means an armchair-shaped hollow carved by ice. A bowl-shaped mountain hollow.

Arête means a sharp ridge between glacial hollows. A narrow ridge between two hollows.

Pyramidal peak means a pointed peak eroded from several sides. Erosion from several sides sharpens a peak.

8–25 min · Teach the Geography

A corrie is a mountain hollow

On screen: A corrie is a bowl-like hollow. / Ice can erode its bed and back wall.

A corrie, also called a cirque, is a bowl-like hollow in a mountain landscape. Snow can collect in a suitable hollow and develop into ice. Erosion can deepen the floor and steepen the back wall, while a rock lip may remain towards the entrance. Point to these parts separately so the word names a landform rather than any mountain lake. Water may occupy a corrie after the ice has gone, but a lake is not required for the hollow to be identified.

Brief check: Is the corrie the ridge or the hollow?
Listen for: The hollow.

An arête is a sharp ridge

On screen: Erosion acts on neighbouring hollows. / A narrow ridge can remain between them.

An arête is a narrow, sharp ridge. When neighbouring corries or glacial valleys erode towards a divide, the ridge between them can become sharper. Show two eroded hollows and trace the remaining high ground. The arête is the material left between the erosion areas, not the bowl itself. This explains why correct labels depend on the part of the landscape being named. Use a finger or pointer to distinguish hollow, wall and ridge before expecting pupils to recall the terminology.

Brief check: Which feature remains between neighbouring eroded hollows?
Listen for: An arête.

Several ridges can meet at a peak

On screen: Erosion can act on several sides. / A sharp peak may remain between them.

Where erosion works around a mountain from several directions, a sharply pointed peak can remain. The common term pyramidal peak describes this form. Compare it with an arête: one is a peak, the other a ridge. Trace each in the diagram and explain how they connect to surrounding hollows. A schematic makes the relationships easier to see but does not prove the complete origin of every real pointed mountain. Rock structure and other processes also affect actual shapes, so apply the terms using relevant landscape evidence.

Brief check: How is a peak different from a ridge?
Listen for: A peak is a summit; a ridge is an extended line of high ground.

Connect each name to the process

On screen: Corrie: hollow. Arête: ridge. / Peak: summit left between eroded areas.

Return to the whole mountain after teaching its parts. Point to one feature and describe its position relative to the others. Then explain which areas were eroded and which high ground remained. This prevents a list of unfamiliar words from replacing understanding. A good description locates the feature, while a good explanation connects it to erosion around it. If a pupil labels the hollow arête, correct the part of the landscape being named rather than merely repeating the vocabulary louder.

Brief check: Why is labelling a hollow “arête” incorrect?
Listen for: The arête is the ridge; the hollow is the corrie.

Build the landforms from the hollow out

On screen: Snow collects in a mountain hollow. / Where several corries erode around a mountain, sharp ridges can meet at a pyramidal peak.

Snow collects in a mountain hollow. As ice develops and moves, erosion deepens the hollow and steepens its back wall, forming a corrie. After melting, water may occupy the hollow as a tarn. If corries erode on opposite sides of a ridge, the narrowing ridge between them can become an arête.

Where several corries erode around a mountain, sharp ridges can meet at a pyramidal peak. The forms are connected by erosion acting from different directions. A corrie is a hollow, an arête a ridge and a peak a summit; learning only their names misses how the shapes relate.

25–32 min · Work through the examples

Worked example · 4.5

On screen: A corrie is an armchair-like hollow shaped by glacial erosion, with a steep back wall. / When neighbouring hollows erode back towards each other, a narrow ridge can remain between them: an arête.

A corrie is an armchair-like hollow shaped by glacial erosion, with a steep back wall. When neighbouring hollows erode back towards each other, a narrow ridge can remain between them: an arête.

The feature is the remaining ridge, not the hollow or a sediment pile.

Where several corries erode around a mountain, sharp ridges can meet at a pyramidal peak. The forms are connected by erosion acting from different directions. A corrie is a hollow, an arête a ridge and a peak a summit; learning only their names misses how the shapes relate.

Explain the contrast

On screen: What does an arête describe?

Response A: A narrow ridge between eroded hollows or valleys.

The feature is the remaining ridge, not the hollow or a sediment pile.

Compare it with response B: A pile of river mud on flat ground.. The difference matters because where several corries erode around a mountain, sharp ridges can meet at a pyramidal peak. The forms are connected by erosion acting from different directions. A corrie is a hollow, an arête a ridge and a peak a summit; learning only their names misses how the shapes relate.

Class board challenge · Explain a corrie and the ridge between hollows

On screen: Follow the teacher’s demonstration on the map.

Snow collects in a mountain hollow. As ice develops and moves, erosion deepens the hollow and steepens its back wall, forming a corrie. After melting, water may occupy the hollow as a tarn. If corries erode on opposite sides of a ridge, the narrowing ridge between them can become an arête.

Where several corries erode around a mountain, sharp ridges can meet at a pyramidal peak. The forms are connected by erosion acting from different directions. A corrie is a hollow, an arête a ridge and a peak a summit; learning only their names misses how the shapes relate.

0–3 min · Introduce the geographical question

Build the landforms from the hollow out

On screen: Is the corrie the ridge or the hollow?

Snow collects in a mountain hollow. As ice develops and moves, erosion deepens the hollow and steepens its back wall, forming a corrie. After melting, water may occupy the hollow as a tarn.

3–5 min · What this lesson explains

Use shape and formation clues together

On screen: Follow the map, diagram and explanation. / No copying is needed. The printed sheet is optional. / A corrie is a bowl-like hollow. / Erosion acts on neighbouring hollows. / Erosion can act on several sides.

This lesson explains how to describe and explain glacial mountain features. The worked example shows the method, and the scheduled case shows how it applies to a different situation. Read the three geographical ideas aloud, then connect each one to a feature in the visual. Students can follow the demonstration without producing a written answer.

5–8 min · Make the words clear

Words we will use

On screen: Corrie: An armchair-shaped hollow carved by ice / Arête: A sharp ridge between glacial hollows / Pyramidal peak: A pointed peak eroded from several sides

Corrie means an armchair-shaped hollow carved by ice. A bowl-shaped mountain hollow.

Arête means a sharp ridge between glacial hollows. A narrow ridge between two hollows.

Pyramidal peak means a pointed peak eroded from several sides. Erosion from several sides sharpens a peak.

8–25 min · Teach the Geography

A corrie is a mountain hollow

On screen: A corrie is a bowl-like hollow. / Ice can erode its bed and back wall.

A corrie, also called a cirque, is a bowl-like hollow in a mountain landscape. Snow can collect in a suitable hollow and develop into ice. Erosion can deepen the floor and steepen the back wall, while a rock lip may remain towards the entrance. Point to these parts separately so the word names a landform rather than any mountain lake. Water may occupy a corrie after the ice has gone, but a lake is not required for the hollow to be identified.

Brief check: Is the corrie the ridge or the hollow?
Listen for: The hollow.

An arête is a sharp ridge

On screen: Erosion acts on neighbouring hollows. / A narrow ridge can remain between them.

An arête is a narrow, sharp ridge. When neighbouring corries or glacial valleys erode towards a divide, the ridge between them can become sharper. Show two eroded hollows and trace the remaining high ground. The arête is the material left between the erosion areas, not the bowl itself. This explains why correct labels depend on the part of the landscape being named. Use a finger or pointer to distinguish hollow, wall and ridge before expecting pupils to recall the terminology.

Brief check: Which feature remains between neighbouring eroded hollows?
Listen for: An arête.

Several ridges can meet at a peak

On screen: Erosion can act on several sides. / A sharp peak may remain between them.

Where erosion works around a mountain from several directions, a sharply pointed peak can remain. The common term pyramidal peak describes this form. Compare it with an arête: one is a peak, the other a ridge. Trace each in the diagram and explain how they connect to surrounding hollows. A schematic makes the relationships easier to see but does not prove the complete origin of every real pointed mountain. Rock structure and other processes also affect actual shapes, so apply the terms using relevant landscape evidence.

Brief check: How is a peak different from a ridge?
Listen for: A peak is a summit; a ridge is an extended line of high ground.

Connect each name to the process

On screen: Corrie: hollow. Arête: ridge. / Peak: summit left between eroded areas.

Return to the whole mountain after teaching its parts. Point to one feature and describe its position relative to the others. Then explain which areas were eroded and which high ground remained. This prevents a list of unfamiliar words from replacing understanding. A good description locates the feature, while a good explanation connects it to erosion around it. If a pupil labels the hollow arête, correct the part of the landscape being named rather than merely repeating the vocabulary louder.

Brief check: Why is labelling a hollow “arête” incorrect?
Listen for: The arête is the ridge; the hollow is the corrie.

Where several corries erode around a mountain, sharp ridges can meet at a pyramidal peak. The forms are connected by erosion acting from different directions. A corrie is a hollow, an arête a ridge and a peak a summit; learning only their names misses how the shapes relate.

What the ice leaves behind

7B · Week 23 · Lesson 1 · sections 4.6

40-minute planning estimate: introduction 3, goal 2, vocabulary 3, explanation 17, worked examples 7, case explanation 4, spoken checks 3, recap 1. Divide each block between topics in combined lessons. Adjust to the class; elapsed classroom teaching time has not been measured.

0–3 min · Introduce the geographical question

Why a boulder can be a traveller

On screen: How does an erratic differ from local bedrock?

A glacier carries debris on its surface, within its ice and at its base. When ice melts, the material can be left behind. Till is often a mixture of sizes deposited directly by ice.

3–5 min · What this lesson explains

Explain deposition when ice loses its load

On screen: Follow the map, diagram and explanation. / No copying is needed. The printed sheet is optional. / An erratic differs from the local bedrock. / Material can travel on, within or beneath ice. / Melting ice releases carried debris.

This lesson explains how to interpret glacial deposits without inventing their age. The worked example shows the method, and the scheduled case shows how it applies to a different situation. Read the three geographical ideas aloud, then connect each one to a feature in the visual. Students can follow the demonstration without producing a written answer.

5–8 min · Make the words clear

Words we will use

On screen: Deposition: Material being dropped / Till: Unsorted material deposited by ice / Moraine: A build-up of debris carried or deposited by a glacier

Deposition means material being dropped. Melting ice releases its debris.

Till means unsorted material deposited by ice. Clay, sand and boulders are mixed together.

Moraine means a build-up of debris carried or deposited by a glacier. Debris can build a ridge at an ice margin.

8–25 min · Teach the Geography

Erratics link deposits to transport

On screen: An erratic differs from the local bedrock. / Its rock type can help investigate where it came from.

A glacial erratic is a transported rock that differs from the local bedrock where it now lies. Its presence can prompt a question about movement from another source area. Compare the rock type with surrounding ground, then investigate a possible matching source and evidence of glacial transport. Difference alone should be interpreted in context rather than used as complete proof of every detail of a journey. An erratic connects the three stages of removal, transport and deposition: the rock began somewhere, moved and was left behind. It also differs from a moraine, which is an accumulation of debris rather than the name for one particular transported block.

Brief check: How does an erratic differ from local bedrock?
Listen for: It has been transported and is of a different rock type from the surrounding bedrock.

Glaciers transport debris

On screen: Material can travel on, within or beneath ice. / Transport differs from its original removal.

Glaciers can carry material in several positions: on the surface, within the ice or near the bed. Rock may enter from erosion beneath the glacier or from valley sides. Removal, transport and deposition are distinct stages. A fragment can be eroded in one place and deposited elsewhere after a period of movement. Trace one fragment through this sequence. Its final location therefore does not automatically show where it originated. This distinction helps explain why deposited material can provide clues about past glacier movement.

Brief check: Does a deposited fragment necessarily come from the place where it now lies?
Listen for: No. It may have been transported.

Deposition leaves material behind

On screen: Melting ice releases carried debris. / Direct glacial deposits can be poorly sorted.

When debris-bearing ice melts, its carried material can be left behind. Directly deposited glacial material, often called till, commonly contains a mixture of particle sizes rather than neatly separated layers. Explain why ice can carry fine and coarse material together. A simple mixed pile models that idea, but real deposits vary and need field evidence. Do not use poor sorting as the only possible clue or assume every mixed deposit is glacial. Interpret it alongside location, landforms and other geological information.

Brief check: What does “poorly sorted” mean here?
Listen for: Different particle sizes are mixed together.

Moraines mark accumulations of debris

On screen: Some lie along glacier sides. / Others form near the front or where ice streams meet.

A moraine is an accumulation of glacial debris. Lateral moraines lie along glacier sides. Where glacier streams join, debris from their adjacent margins can form a medial moraine. Accumulations near an end position include terminal or end moraines. Use location to distinguish the names instead of treating them as separate kinds of rock. A ridge of debris may help reconstruct a former ice margin, but interpreting its age and origin needs appropriate evidence. The visible position is the starting observation, not the entire historical conclusion.

Brief check: What helps distinguish lateral and end moraines?
Listen for: Their positions relative to the glacier.

Meltwater can sort sediment

On screen: Moving water carries different sizes differently. / Sorted layers may reflect meltwater deposition.

Meltwater flows away from ice and can transport and deposit sediment. Flowing water can sort particles because different sizes and densities settle under different conditions. A strongly layered, sorted deposit therefore raises a different interpretation from a simple direct release of mixed debris by melting ice. Location near a glacier does not mean every deposit was laid down directly by ice. Compare the mechanisms and ask which observations each predicts. The answer should match the deposit’s features and context rather than rely only on the region’s label.

Brief check: What alternative should we consider for sorted sediment near a glacier?
Listen for: Transport and deposition by meltwater.

Why a boulder can be a traveller

On screen: A glacier carries debris on its surface, within its ice and at its base. / An erratic is a transported rock unlike the local bedrock.

A glacier carries debris on its surface, within its ice and at its base. When ice melts, the material can be left behind. Till is often a mixture of sizes deposited directly by ice. Moraine describes an accumulation of glacial debris, such as a ridge beside or at the end of a glacier.

An erratic is a transported rock unlike the local bedrock. Its composition can help connect it to a source area. Meltwater can sort sediment by flow conditions, so not every glacial deposit is an unsorted mixture. Distinguish the material, its arrangement and the process that deposited it.

Direct deposition by ice need not sort particles like flowing meltwater can.

Its composition can help connect it to a source area. Meltwater can sort sediment by flow conditions, so not every glacial deposit is an unsorted mixture. Distinguish the material, its arrangement and the process that deposited it.
