7B · Week 37 · Lesson 1 · sections 5.8, 5.9, 5.10

40-minute planning estimate: introduction 3, goal 2, vocabulary 3, explanation 17, worked examples 7, case explanation 4, spoken checks 3, recap 1. Divide each block between topics in combined lessons. Adjust to the class; elapsed classroom teaching time has not been measured.

0–3 min · Introduce the geographical question

Same rain, faster response

On screen: Is every flood caused by the same process?

Compare two invented runoff trials with 30 water units of rain each. In A, 18 infiltrate and 12 become runoff. In B, 6 infiltrate and 24 become runoff.

Turn a flood report into an explanation

On screen: Can an invented count be reported as a verified historical Thames figure?

A flood explanation connects causes, pathways and consequences. Prolonged rain may saturate soils, reducing further infiltration. More rapid runoff can enter channels; when flow exceeds capacity, water spreads beyond the banks.

A defence changes where water can go

On screen: Does having a flood measure guarantee zero risk?

An embankment can keep water within a channel up to its design conditions. Flood storage creates space for water temporarily, while warnings help people act before an event. These measures work through different mechanisms.

3–5 min · What this lesson explains

Connect causes to impacts through a mechanism

On screen: Follow the map, diagram and explanation. / No copying is needed. The printed sheet is optional. / A channel can overflow. / Saturated ground has less available storage. / Paving can reduce infiltration locally.

This lesson explains how to connect rainfall pathways to flood risk. The worked example shows the method, and the scheduled case shows how it applies to a different situation. Read the three geographical ideas aloud, then connect each one to a feature in the visual. Students can follow the demonstration without producing a written answer.

Organise a case file without mixing fact and invention

On screen: Follow the map, diagram and explanation. / No copying is needed. The printed sheet is optional. / Separate real facts from classroom figures. / Cause → process → impact. / It helps protect London from tidal and combined flood risk.

This lesson explains how to organise a flood case using trustworthy evidence. The worked example shows the method, and the scheduled case shows how it applies to a different situation. Read the three geographical ideas aloud, then connect each one to a feature in the visual. Students can follow the demonstration without producing a written answer.

Evaluate performance after checking affordability

On screen: Follow the map, diagram and explanation. / No copying is needed. The printed sheet is optional. / Measures have different purposes. / Structures can alter channels or barriers. / Add the complete package cost.

This lesson explains how to recommend flood measures with reasons and limits. The worked example shows the method, and the scheduled case shows how it applies to a different situation. Read the three geographical ideas aloud, then connect each one to a feature in the visual. Students can follow the demonstration without producing a written answer.

5–8 min · Make the words clear

Words we will use

On screen: Flood: Water covering normally dry land / Runoff: Water flowing over the land surface / Infiltration: Water soaking into the ground

Flood means water covering normally dry land. Water spreads beyond the channel.

Runoff means water flowing over the land surface. Water moves across a paved surface.

Infiltration means water soaking into the ground. Water enters pores in soil.

Words we will use

On screen: Cause: A factor contributing to an event / Impact: An effect of the event / Response: An action taken before, during or after

Cause means a factor contributing to an event. Prolonged rain adds water to a basin.

Impact means an effect of the event. Overflow damages homes or closes a road.

Response means an action taken before, during or after. Warnings help people prepare.

Words we will use

On screen: Flood defence: A measure intended to reduce flood risk / Warning: Information helping people prepare / Risk: The likelihood and consequences of harm

Flood defence means a measure intended to reduce flood risk. A wall may reduce local overflow.

Warning means information helping people prepare. A notice can prompt action before a flood.

Risk means the likelihood and consequences of harm. Exposure and consequences matter with likelihood.

8–25 min · Reconnect and explain

Flooding means water covers normally dry land

On screen: A channel can overflow. / Other flood mechanisms also exist.

Flooding occurs when water covers land that is normally dry. A river can overflow when water exceeds the capacity of its channel at a location. Surface-water flooding can also occur when drainage cannot remove water quickly enough. Coastal conditions can create other mechanisms. Start with the source’s actual process rather than assuming every flood has the same cause. A risk explanation should connect water input, movement or storage to where people and property are exposed. This makes the difference between naming rain and explaining how flooding develops.

Brief check: Is every flood caused by the same process?
Listen for: No. The mechanism must be identified.

Land use can change the response

On screen: Paving can reduce infiltration locally. / Drainage can route water differently.

Replacing permeable ground with paving can reduce local infiltration and alter runoff pathways. Drains may move water quickly towards a channel, although the outcome depends on design and conditions. Compare the same rainfall input before and after a surface change so pupils understand the mechanism being tested. Do not say identical rainfall guarantees identical runoff. The surface and drainage system mediate the response. A real explanation requires evidence of the relevant land-use and drainage changes rather than inferring them from a flood photograph alone.

Brief check: Can runoff change even if rainfall stays the same?
Listen for: Yes. Surface and drainage conditions can change.

Causes and impacts are different

On screen: Cause: a factor contributing to flooding. / Impact: what happens because of the event.

Heavy rain and restricted channel capacity can contribute to a flood. Damaged homes, closed roads and interrupted services are impacts. Build the sequence from trigger through pathway to outcome. “Rain caused damage” skips the process that connects them. Impacts also depend on what is exposed and how people can respond. Two floods with similar water levels can produce different harm if buildings, warning systems or access differ. Describe immediate and later impacts separately so repairs and lost activity do not become confused with the initial flood mechanism.

Brief check: Are damaged homes a cause or an impact?
Listen for: An impact.

Same rain, faster response

On screen: Compare two invented runoff trials with 30 water units of rain each. / Flooding occurs when water exceeds channel or drainage capacity, or collects where it cannot drain.

Compare two invented runoff trials with 30 water units of rain each. In A, 18 infiltrate and 12 become runoff. In B, 6 infiltrate and 24 become runoff. Rainfall is unchanged; runoff doubles. Where less water enters the ground and more reaches channels quickly, river levels may respond faster.

Flooding occurs when water exceeds channel or drainage capacity, or collects where it cannot drain. Antecedent wetness, rainfall duration, basin shape and available storage also matter. Paving can increase rapid runoff in some settings, but one puddle photograph cannot prove which factor caused a particular flood.

A case study needs a trustworthy source

On screen: Separate real facts from classroom figures. / Name the event, place and source.

A case study connects processes to a particular place and event. Real dates and counts need sources that support them. Our invented flood log practises organising an explanation, but it must not become a historical claim about the Thames. State which information is factual background and which belongs to the fictional exercise. This distinction allows meaningful practice without misleading pupils. A neat table or detailed number does not make a source authentic; provenance concerns where the information came from and what it represents.

Brief check: Can an invented count be reported as a verified historical Thames figure?
Listen for: No. It belongs to the fictional exercise.

The Thames Barrier has a specific role

On screen: It helps protect London from tidal and combined flood risk. / It does not stop every flood across the basin.

The Thames Barrier helps protect London against tidal and combined tidal and river flood risk under its operating arrangements. Its location and mechanism matter. It is not a device that removes every rainstorm, clears every drain or prevents all upstream flooding. Compare a barrier, a blocked local drain and rainfall farther upstream. Each problem has a different pathway and may require a different response. Teaching the barrier’s real role accurately is more useful than calling it a universal solution or suggesting it has no benefit because it has limits.

Brief check: Would a tidal barrier automatically clear a blocked local drain?
Listen for: No. It addresses a different mechanism.

Match responses to mechanisms

On screen: Warnings help people prepare. / Drainage maintenance and repairs address different needs.

A response should address the source’s actual problem. Warning residents can help them act, but they also need time, information and practical means to respond. Drainage maintenance can address a blockage; it does not guarantee protection from every river flood. Repairs address damage after the event rather than preventing the original trigger. Ask what each response changes and what it leaves unchanged. This mechanism-based comparison supports an informed recommendation without assuming that the most familiar named measure is always the right one.

Brief check: Why can a warning be insufficient on its own?
Listen for: People may lack the transport, time or means to act.

Turn a flood report into an explanation

On screen: A flood explanation connects causes, pathways and consequences. / Separate the hazard from exposure: the flood is the event, while people and property in affected places are exposed.

A flood explanation connects causes, pathways and consequences. Prolonged rain may saturate soils, reducing further infiltration. More rapid runoff can enter channels; when flow exceeds capacity, water spreads beyond the banks. Houses, roads or fields in its path may be damaged. Each link explains how the next effect can occur.

Separate the hazard from exposure: the flood is the event, while people and property in affected places are exposed. A photograph shows visible conditions at a moment. Rainfall records, water levels and dated reports help explain the event. Warnings can reduce harm even when they do not prevent water rising.

Flood management aims to reduce risk

On screen: Measures have different purposes. / No single measure guarantees zero risk.

Flood management can seek to reduce the likelihood of flooding, reduce exposure or help people prepare and recover. Different measures act on different parts of that chain. Storage may hold water temporarily; barriers may limit a particular inflow; warning systems help people respond. Start by identifying the flood mechanism and affected area. The existence of a measure does not mean all risk disappears. Its capacity, location, maintenance and the event conditions influence performance. A realistic explanation names the intended benefit and the limits that remain.

Brief check: Does having a flood measure guarantee zero risk?
Listen for: No. Capacity and conditions still matter.

A feasible package must fit the shared budget

On screen: Add the complete package cost. / Affordability comes before comparing preferences.

If a package includes warnings, storage and a wall, add all their costs. Checking that each item individually costs less than the budget is insufficient. A fifty-token budget cannot fund a sixty-token total. Once feasibility is established, compare how well the package addresses the actual risks. The cheapest package may fail to protect the required area, while the most expensive feasible one may create unnecessary costs. Our tokens are invented classroom data; real costs and permissions require appropriate information beyond the model.

Brief check: What is wrong with checking only each individual price?
Listen for: The combined package can exceed the shared budget.

Evaluate effects across places and time

On screen: Who benefits? Who may face new risk? / What maintenance and evidence are needed?

A flood wall may protect one neighbourhood but shift faster flow towards another. A responsible evaluation includes that transferred risk rather than counting only the local benefit. Consider the system, affected groups, long-term maintenance and environmental effects. A larger budget creates options but does not prove which is best. State what further evidence would help, such as flow modelling, capacity or land-use information. Invite opinions about priorities after explaining the supported outcomes. A recommendation should make its reasoning and remaining uncertainty clear enough to review.

Brief check: Does a benefit at one site establish a benefit everywhere?
Listen for: No. Effects can be uneven or transferred.

A defence changes where water can go

On screen: An embankment can keep water within a channel up to its design conditions. / No measure makes risk zero.

An embankment can keep water within a channel up to its design conditions. Flood storage creates space for water temporarily, while warnings help people act before an event. These measures work through different mechanisms. A wall, a storage area and a warning system are not interchangeable protections.

No measure makes risk zero. Defences can be exceeded, storage can fill and warnings need time and a usable response. Compare maintenance, residual risk, upstream and downstream effects, costs and who benefits. The most expensive package is not automatically the most effective for the stated location.

Flooding occurs when water exceeds channel or drainage capacity, or collects where it cannot drain. Antecedent wetness, rainfall duration, basin shape and available storage also matter. Paving can increase rapid runoff in some settings, but one puddle photograph cannot prove which factor caused a particular flood.

An impact.

What this case teaches

On screen: Separate real facts from classroom figures. / As a figure from the fictional exercise.

Separate the hazard from exposure: the flood is the event, while people and property in affected places are exposed. A photograph shows visible conditions at a moment. Rainfall records, water levels and dated reports help explain the event. Warnings can reduce harm even when they do not prevent water rising.

People may lack the transport, time or means to act.

On screen: Measures have different purposes. / Suitability and effects supported by local evidence.

7B · Week 37 · Lesson 2 · sections 5.8, 5.9, 5.10

40-minute planning estimate: introduction 3, goal 2, vocabulary 3, explanation 17, worked examples 7, case explanation 4, spoken checks 3, recap 1. Divide each block between topics in combined lessons. Adjust to the class; elapsed classroom teaching time has not been measured.

0–3 min · Introduce the geographical question

Same rain, faster response

On screen: Is every flood caused by the same process?

Compare two invented runoff trials with 30 water units of rain each. In A, 18 infiltrate and 12 become runoff. In B, 6 infiltrate and 24 become runoff.

Turn a flood report into an explanation

On screen: Can an invented count be reported as a verified historical Thames figure?

A flood explanation connects causes, pathways and consequences. Prolonged rain may saturate soils, reducing further infiltration. More rapid runoff can enter channels; when flow exceeds capacity, water spreads beyond the banks.

A defence changes where water can go

On screen: Does having a flood measure guarantee zero risk?

An embankment can keep water within a channel up to its design conditions. Flood storage creates space for water temporarily, while warnings help people act before an event. These measures work through different mechanisms.

3–5 min · What this lesson explains

Control one variable in a runoff experiment

On screen: Follow the map, diagram and explanation. / No copying is needed. The printed sheet is optional. / A channel can overflow. / Saturated ground has less available storage. / Paving can reduce infiltration locally.

This lesson explains how to connect rainfall pathways to flood risk. The worked example shows the method, and the scheduled case shows how it applies to a different situation. Read the three geographical ideas aloud, then connect each one to a feature in the visual. Students can follow the demonstration without producing a written answer.

Match a response to the flood mechanism

On screen: Follow the map, diagram and explanation. / No copying is needed. The printed sheet is optional. / Separate real facts from classroom figures. / Cause → process → impact. / It helps protect London from tidal and combined flood risk.

This lesson explains how to organise a flood case using trustworthy evidence. The worked example shows the method, and the scheduled case shows how it applies to a different situation. Read the three geographical ideas aloud, then connect each one to a feature in the visual. Students can follow the demonstration without producing a written answer.

Choose a feasible package and explain its limits

On screen: Follow the map, diagram and explanation. / No copying is needed. The printed sheet is optional. / Measures have different purposes. / Structures can alter channels or barriers. / Add the complete package cost.

This lesson explains how to recommend flood measures with reasons and limits. The worked example shows the method, and the scheduled case shows how it applies to a different situation. Read the three geographical ideas aloud, then connect each one to a feature in the visual. Students can follow the demonstration without producing a written answer.

5–8 min · Make the words clear

Words we will use

On screen: Flood: Water covering normally dry land / Runoff: Water flowing over the land surface / Infiltration: Water soaking into the ground

Flood means water covering normally dry land. Water spreads beyond the channel.

Runoff means water flowing over the land surface. Water moves across a paved surface.

Infiltration means water soaking into the ground. Water enters pores in soil.

Words we will use

On screen: Cause: A factor contributing to an event / Impact: An effect of the event / Response: An action taken before, during or after

Cause means a factor contributing to an event. Prolonged rain adds water to a basin.

Impact means an effect of the event. Overflow damages homes or closes a road.

Response means an action taken before, during or after. Warnings help people prepare.

Words we will use

On screen: Flood defence: A measure intended to reduce flood risk / Warning: Information helping people prepare / Risk: The likelihood and consequences of harm

Flood defence means a measure intended to reduce flood risk. A wall may reduce local overflow.

Warning means information helping people prepare. A notice can prompt action before a flood.

Risk means the likelihood and consequences of harm. Exposure and consequences matter with likelihood.

8–25 min · Reconnect and explain

Flooding means water covers normally dry land

On screen: A channel can overflow. / Other flood mechanisms also exist.

Flooding occurs when water covers land that is normally dry. A river can overflow when water exceeds the capacity of its channel at a location. Surface-water flooding can also occur when drainage cannot remove water quickly enough. Coastal conditions can create other mechanisms. Start with the source’s actual process rather than assuming every flood has the same cause. A risk explanation should connect water input, movement or storage to where people and property are exposed. This makes the difference between naming rain and explaining how flooding develops.

Brief check: Is every flood caused by the same process?
Listen for: No. The mechanism must be identified.

Land use can change the response

On screen: Paving can reduce infiltration locally. / Drainage can route water differently.

Replacing permeable ground with paving can reduce local infiltration and alter runoff pathways. Drains may move water quickly towards a channel, although the outcome depends on design and conditions. Compare the same rainfall input before and after a surface change so pupils understand the mechanism being tested. Do not say identical rainfall guarantees identical runoff. The surface and drainage system mediate the response. A real explanation requires evidence of the relevant land-use and drainage changes rather than inferring them from a flood photograph alone.

Brief check: Can runoff change even if rainfall stays the same?
Listen for: Yes. Surface and drainage conditions can change.

Causes and impacts are different

On screen: Cause: a factor contributing to flooding. / Impact: what happens because of the event.

Heavy rain and restricted channel capacity can contribute to a flood. Damaged homes, closed roads and interrupted services are impacts. Build the sequence from trigger through pathway to outcome. “Rain caused damage” skips the process that connects them. Impacts also depend on what is exposed and how people can respond. Two floods with similar water levels can produce different harm if buildings, warning systems or access differ. Describe immediate and later impacts separately so repairs and lost activity do not become confused with the initial flood mechanism.

Brief check: Are damaged homes a cause or an impact?
Listen for: An impact.

Same rain, faster response

On screen: Compare two invented runoff trials with 30 water units of rain each. / Flooding occurs when water exceeds channel or drainage capacity, or collects where it cannot drain.

Compare two invented runoff trials with 30 water units of rain each. In A, 18 infiltrate and 12 become runoff. In B, 6 infiltrate and 24 become runoff. Rainfall is unchanged; runoff doubles. Where less water enters the ground and more reaches channels quickly, river levels may respond faster.

Flooding occurs when water exceeds channel or drainage capacity, or collects where it cannot drain. Antecedent wetness, rainfall duration, basin shape and available storage also matter. Paving can increase rapid runoff in some settings, but one puddle photograph cannot prove which factor caused a particular flood.

A case study needs a trustworthy source

On screen: Separate real facts from classroom figures. / Name the event, place and source.

A case study connects processes to a particular place and event. Real dates and counts need sources that support them. Our invented flood log practises organising an explanation, but it must not become a historical claim about the Thames. State which information is factual background and which belongs to the fictional exercise. This distinction allows meaningful practice without misleading pupils. A neat table or detailed number does not make a source authentic; provenance concerns where the information came from and what it represents.

Brief check: Can an invented count be reported as a verified historical Thames figure?
Listen for: No. It belongs to the fictional exercise.

The Thames Barrier has a specific role

On screen: It helps protect London from tidal and combined flood risk. / It does not stop every flood across the basin.

The Thames Barrier helps protect London against tidal and combined tidal and river flood risk under its operating arrangements. Its location and mechanism matter. It is not a device that removes every rainstorm, clears every drain or prevents all upstream flooding. Compare a barrier, a blocked local drain and rainfall farther upstream. Each problem has a different pathway and may require a different response. Teaching the barrier’s real role accurately is more useful than calling it a universal solution or suggesting it has no benefit because it has limits.

Brief check: Would a tidal barrier automatically clear a blocked local drain?
Listen for: No. It addresses a different mechanism.

Match responses to mechanisms

On screen: Warnings help people prepare. / Drainage maintenance and repairs address different needs.

A response should address the source’s actual problem. Warning residents can help them act, but they also need time, information and practical means to respond. Drainage maintenance can address a blockage; it does not guarantee protection from every river flood. Repairs address damage after the event rather than preventing the original trigger. Ask what each response changes and what it leaves unchanged. This mechanism-based comparison supports an informed recommendation without assuming that the most familiar named measure is always the right one.

Brief check: Why can a warning be insufficient on its own?
Listen for: People may lack the transport, time or means to act.

Turn a flood report into an explanation

On screen: A flood explanation connects causes, pathways and consequences. / Separate the hazard from exposure: the flood is the event, while people and property in affected places are exposed.

A flood explanation connects causes, pathways and consequences. Prolonged rain may saturate soils, reducing further infiltration. More rapid runoff can enter channels; when flow exceeds capacity, water spreads beyond the banks. Houses, roads or fields in its path may be damaged. Each link explains how the next effect can occur.

Separate the hazard from exposure: the flood is the event, while people and property in affected places are exposed. A photograph shows visible conditions at a moment. Rainfall records, water levels and dated reports help explain the event. Warnings can reduce harm even when they do not prevent water rising.

Flood management aims to reduce risk

On screen: Measures have different purposes. / No single measure guarantees zero risk.

Flood management can seek to reduce the likelihood of flooding, reduce exposure or help people prepare and recover. Different measures act on different parts of that chain. Storage may hold water temporarily; barriers may limit a particular inflow; warning systems help people respond. Start by identifying the flood mechanism and affected area. The existence of a measure does not mean all risk disappears. Its capacity, location, maintenance and the event conditions influence performance. A realistic explanation names the intended benefit and the limits that remain.

Brief check: Does having a flood measure guarantee zero risk?
Listen for: No. Capacity and conditions still matter.

A feasible package must fit the shared budget

On screen: Add the complete package cost. / Affordability comes before comparing preferences.

If a package includes warnings, storage and a wall, add all their costs. Checking that each item individually costs less than the budget is insufficient. A fifty-token budget cannot fund a sixty-token total. Once feasibility is established, compare how well the package addresses the actual risks. The cheapest package may fail to protect the required area, while the most expensive feasible one may create unnecessary costs. Our tokens are invented classroom data; real costs and permissions require appropriate information beyond the model.

Brief check: What is wrong with checking only each individual price?
Listen for: The combined package can exceed the shared budget.

Evaluate effects across places and time

On screen: Who benefits? Who may face new risk? / What maintenance and evidence are needed?

A flood wall may protect one neighbourhood but shift faster flow towards another. A responsible evaluation includes that transferred risk rather than counting only the local benefit. Consider the system, affected groups, long-term maintenance and environmental effects. A larger budget creates options but does not prove which is best. State what further evidence would help, such as flow modelling, capacity or land-use information. Invite opinions about priorities after explaining the supported outcomes. A recommendation should make its reasoning and remaining uncertainty clear enough to review.

Brief check: Does a benefit at one site establish a benefit everywhere?
Listen for: No. Effects can be uneven or transferred.

A defence changes where water can go

On screen: An embankment can keep water within a channel up to its design conditions. / No measure makes risk zero.

An embankment can keep water within a channel up to its design conditions. Flood storage creates space for water temporarily, while warnings help people act before an event. These measures work through different mechanisms. A wall, a storage area and a warning system are not interchangeable protections.

No measure makes risk zero. Defences can be exceeded, storage can fill and warnings need time and a usable response. Compare maintenance, residual risk, upstream and downstream effects, costs and who benefits. The most expensive package is not automatically the most effective for the stated location.

Change the example · 5.8

The question is: Double the rain while keeping the percentages. What happens?

Both model quantities double. The simplified model keeps the proportions fixed.
